    But here, it’s worth saying that satellites in low orbit are much cheaper to put in place, which also explains the sheer volume SpaceX has been able to launch in recent years.

    With far fewer satellites, but in higher orbit, Europeans can also cover the whole planet. It’s just that the system isn’t as flexible.

    Finally, is money part of the explanation? Yes, of course. The United States spends around six times more on its space programmes, civil and military, than Europeans do.

    There’s also another factor that helps SpaceX deploy thousands of satellites at low cost: it has its own launcher, the Falcon 9.

    Eutelsat, on the other hand, has to buy launches from third parties. So it’s much more expensive, and it doesn’t control the pace at which it can put satellites into orbit.

    Before wrapping up, a quick word about China, another big actor. It’s quite new in the space industry, and it’s not really spending huge amounts of money for the moment. But it’s worth keeping an eye on Beijing on this front too.

    Neither Ukrainian nor independent sources confirm the Russian reports of Ukrainian attacks in this area, but given past experience, it is possible that this is the result of the Ukrainian army’s operational silence.

    The more likely explanation, however, is different.

    As it has done many times in recent months, Rybar is “retreating” with its maps from entirely unrealistic positions that it, together with other Russian accounts, had drawn months earlier on the basis of reports from the defence ministry.

    Far more credible sources, meanwhile, see the situation as even less favourable for the Russians than they themselves are willing to admit. The OSINT Playfra account marks both Zarichne and Yampil as grey zones, while Torske lies directly on its border. Rybar marks all three villages as controlled by the Russian army.

    The situation is very similar according to the Finns from Black Bird Group:

    During talks in Abu Dhabi, the Russians argued using their fabricated maps. Based on reports from members of the Ukrainian delegation, this is claimed by president Volodymyr Zelensky.

    They told Kyiv that members of the Russian team believe their army has already occupied half of the remaining territory of Donbas controlled by the Ukrainian army.

    “These were military officers, Russian intelligence, and they were serious about it. Our team told them, ‘We don’t know how you can even say such things. We have video footage, images, other things proving that these areas are under our control,’” Zelensky said of the talks.

    On that basis, he claims that Russian president Vladimir Putin lives in a different reality, which is a problem for the talks. According to Zelensky, however, the American delegation confirmed the Ukrainian version of the state of the front line.

    The possibility, which the Ukrainian president wrote about, that Putin is simply being lied to, is only one possible explanation. The other is a deliberate decision to insist on unrealistic claims and to derive the future demarcation line from them.

    What this may mean in the case of Lyman, mentioned above, is shown by the official map of the Russian state press agency Ria Novosti from Wednesday (11 November 2026). Not only is Lyman (in Russian, Krasny Liman) marked as captured on it, but according to the Kremlin, Putin’s August statement that the Russians had also captured Sviatohirsk, far to the west, still stands.

    In reality, the front is more than 30 km further east at this point. But because Putin claims something different, according to Russia the situation is quite different. We do not know whether this is one of the areas Zelensky wrote about, but it is very likely, and there are more such places across the entire front.

    This is how the same area looks according to Playfra. Sviatohirsk is in the upper left half of both images:

    The monitored Russian sources have not yet directly commented on Zelensky’s post, but Rybar, for example, generally states that the outcome of the talks will be determined by reality on the ground, while positions differ on the question of Donbas: “The Russian side demands all of it and refuses to give up what it controls.”

    The problem is that it controls far less than it claims. If this does not change, Moscow can drag out the talks for as long as it wants.

    Russian incursions into Kupiansk continue. “On the Kupiansk axis, intense fighting continues, including fighting directly in the city. The presence of Russian soldiers has been recorded in several parts of the city: in the north-west, on the western edge, in the area of the Yubileinyi settlement, as well as in individual neighbourhoods,” the Ukrainian account Petrenko writes.

    The same source confirms the presence of Russians in the village of Myrove as well, which lies directly on the north-western border of Kupiansk (on Petrenko’s map, Myrove is in the upper left).

    Nevertheless, the author claims that although heavy fighting is taking place, there has been no significant change in the front line recently. He himself, however, expanded the grey zone to cover almost the entire city, meaning that the Russians have once again gained the upper hand there.

    Four American cruise missiles were reportedly shot down over Russian territory. After almost five years of war, this already sounds like an ordinary report, but given US president Donald Trump’s openly pro-Russian stance, it is far more interesting. The Russians claim that they managed to shoot down four AGM-188A Rusty Dagger cruise missiles.

    Its development began in the summer of 2024, and it was planned as a cheap weapon for striking targets on Russian territory. It was being developed by lesser-known American and European companies, and it was assumed that Norway, Denmark and the Netherlands would pay for its purchase.

    The missile carries a 227-kg warhead, has stealth features and increased resistance to electronic jamming. The fact that the Russian army has just announced four successes does not mean that the AGM-188A has not been deployed before. It is possible that some of the successful attacks in previous months were carried out precisely with this weapon.

    The Russians, for example, claim that they discovered components of the new weapon after the June attack in the rubble of the hit arsenal in Voronezh. It was initially speculated that it had been destroyed by British-French Storm Shadow/SCALP-EG missiles.

    On Tuesday, the Russians published a map showing how large a part of their territory the AMG-188A is capable of striking with its maximum range of 930 km. The map was published by the well-known channel Fighterbomber, but it was created by the propaganda agency Sputnik.

    It also serves well as an illustration of the main theme of today’s Ukraine Battlefield update. Not only the territory of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions is marked as Russian on it, but also the entire Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions.

    In this case, these are not fabricated successes of the Russian army, but Sputnik is adhering to the Russian constitution, which, after the manipulated referendums in the autumn of 2022, declared all four regions to be full-fledged Russian territory.

    Videos of the day

    On 11 November 2022, the Ukrainian army entered liberated Kherson. There are many videos in which enthusiastic local residents welcome it. They showed courage immediately after the occupation, when they repeatedly demonstrated against the Russian army directly in the city.

    Four years after liberation, a large part of the city lies in ruins, the Russians systematically bomb it, and drone operators pursue even civilian residents in its streets. Most of them have fled.

    The Russians showed how they use Mi-28 attack helicopters to launch light Banderol cruise missiles.

    The same thing is happening to Sloviansk as to all the cities attacked by the Russian army — it is ceasing to exist.

    The launch of a missile from the S-300 system. The rocket motor ignites only after it has left the launch device. The tubes containing the missiles always point vertically upwards in firing position; the missile takes its intended direction only after the motor is ignited.

    RAND Corporation analyst Michael Bohnert created an illustrative simulation from the perspective of the crew of a Russian short-range Pantsir system, which typically directly guards important targets.

    His aim was to demonstrate clearly how much the speed of a drone affects the reaction time of air-defence systems. The first flying object is the most common Ukrainian FP-1 drone, flying at a speed of 160 km/h at an altitude of 30 metres above the ground. The second is a Flamingo cruise missile flying at a speed of 500 km/h at the same altitude.

    What are the losses

    No update on Wednesday.

    • By Monday (9 November), Russia had verifiably lost 24,275 pieces of heavy equipment (on Monday, 2 November, it was 24,251). Of these, 19,240 (19,216) pieces were destroyed by the Ukrainians, 1,001 (1,001) were damaged, 1,192 (1,192) were abandoned by their crews and 2,842 (2,842) were captured by the Ukrainian army. Of these, 4,456 (4,454) are tanks, of which 3,361 (3,359) were destroyed in combat.
    • Ukraine lost 12,346 (12,320) pieces of equipment, of which 9,736 (9,711) were destroyed, 719 (718) damaged, 693 (693) abandoned and 1,198 (1,198) captured. Of these, 1,473 (1,473) are tanks, of which 1,133 (1,133) were destroyed in combat.

    Note: Neither side regularly reports its dead or destroyed equipment. Ukraine publishes daily figures for Russian casualties and destroyed equipment, which cannot be independently verified. This overview uses data from the Oryx project, which has been compiling a list of exclusively photographically documented equipment losses since the beginning of the war.

    ]]>

      <description><p>Problem affects businesses, government agencies and even tech firm’s own employees</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage-outlook-teams-word-excel-reports">Microsoft scrambles to fix global outage affecting Teams and Outlook</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/live/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage-down-today-live-update-outlook-teams-365-when-fixed-latest-status-cause-news">Microsoft outage – live updates</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/13/tell-us-have-you-been-affected-by-the-microsoft-outage">Tell us: have you been affected by the Microsoft outage?</a></p></li></ul><p>Millions of people were unable to access their emails, Teams chats or meetings on Thursday night and Friday morning after a Microsoft 365 outage brought down services across the globe.</p><p>The incident affected businesses, government agencies and even Microsoft employees.       <title>A timeline of the affair scandal that sank Nvidia’s Jensen Huang</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/12/jensen-huang-affair-timeline</link>
      <description><p>CEO behind the meteoric rise of Nvidia stepped down after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy </p><p>Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/nvidia">Nvidia</a>, the company at the center of the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/artificialintelligenceai">AI</a> boom, after leading it for more than 30 years.</p><p>Huang, an electrical engineer by education, stewarded the company from a $1bn firm when it went public in 1999 to a company valued at more than $4tn in 2026. But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/12/jensen-huang-affair-timeline">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Rallies will take place on more than US 40 campuses as workers seeking better pay and conditions decry stalled talks</p><p>Starbucks baristas, students, elected officials and allies are planning rallies at <a href="https://starbucksworkersunited.controlshift.app/events?link_id=2&amp;can_id=debd8d2ad19f005d15f9bbdff314d42a&amp;source=email-nov-12-day-of-action-for-starbucks-baristas&amp;email_referrer=email_3490793&amp;email_subject=nov-12-day-of-action-for-starbucks-baristas&amp;&amp;">over 40 college campuses</a> across the US on Thursday to support the Starbucks Workers United <a href="https://www.boycottstarbucks.net/">boycott campaign</a> as the union nears five years of deadlock with the company over contract negotiations.</p><p>Starbucks Workers United is <a href="https://sbworkersunited.org/what-were-fighting-for-updates-on-contract-bargaining/">seeking</a> better pay and stronger staffing levels, including a $17 an hour minimum wage for baristas and a minimum staffing of three workers per store.       <description><p>Sales of built units fell to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, with mortgage rates at nearly three-year high</p><p>US existing home sales hit a 16-year low in October as buyers were driven away by record-high <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/money/mortgage-rates">mortgage rates</a> and rising inflation, according to new data released on Wednesday.</p><p>Sales of already built units dropped to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, the National Association of Realtors (NAR) reported. The median existing-home sales price increased slightly to $416,700.       <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/11/democrats-election-medicaid-costs</link>
      <description><p>‘The post-election wish list is about to run into harsh fiscal reality: there is no money’</p><p>Is this an opportunity for a new America? As the Reagan revolution four decades ago launched US society down the path to low taxes and meager solidarity, perhaps the Republican bloodbath last week could turn US politics toward building a new social contract anchored on an aspiration to equitable prosperity.</p><p>One can sense the ambition of the bumper new crop of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/democrats">Democrats</a> ushered to power last week, calling for support for programs for children and their parents; emphatically endorsing the long-held dream of Medicare for All. The project includes rolling back <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s cuts to Medicaid and food stamps, and restoring subsidies for health insurance under the Affordable Care Act that Republicans allowed to expire. And that’s just the start.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/11/democrats-election-medicaid-costs">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Trump-appointed judge Jeffrey T Kuntz partially denies British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss over edit</p><p>Federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz ruled on Tuesday that Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the BBC can proceed, denying in part the British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss the case.       <title>Farewell to Elon Musk’s Cybertruck. Has any car ever been more repellent? | Arwa Mahdawi</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/11/farewell-cybertruck-elon-musk-car-repellent</link>
      <description><p>Safety campaigners have condemned it and owners have complained about it. Goodbye to a steel monstrosity seemingly designed by a five-year-old</p><p>Elon Musk is having a rough go of it, isn’t he? The world’s richest man spent almost half a billion dollars on the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/04/elon-musk-midterm-spending-analysis">midterms</a> in a failed attempt to defend Republican control of government. Now the tech mogul, who moved from California to Texas to escape Democrats and regulations, finds himself in a newly blue state. He also finds himself the subject of an unflattering <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/08/musk-review-epic-study-worlds-richest-most-banal-man-elon-film">documentary</a> and, if the Democrats follow through on threats to investigate him, could potentially be in a spot of legal bother.</p><p>And to top it all off? Musk’s beloved Cybertruck, the steel monstrosity that looks as if it were designed by a five-year-old, is <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/06/tesla-to-wind-down-cybertruck-production-as-elon-musk-focuses-on-robotics-and-ai">winding down production</a>. According to Musk, this isn’t because it’s an abject failure, but because he is channelling his energy into other things. “This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media,” Musk <a href="https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2119691615774146614?a=pN3ISFVZZ-aU4_-TlJw&amp;s=20">tweeted</a> on Monday. “But rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.” (The Cybercab is a two-passenger robotaxi.)</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/11/farewell-cybertruck-elon-musk-car-repellent">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comFri, 13 Nov 2026 14:46:09 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Take the time to prepare for retirement ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/13/take-the-time-to-prepare-for-retirement/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/13/take-the-time-to-prepare-for-retirement/Fri, 13 Nov 2026 14:29:54 +0000Getting your finances straight, prioritising your mental and physical health and finding enjoyable ways to spend your time are key to a happy retirement

If you’ve spent years working for the boss from hell, then it’s likely retirement can’t come fast enough. But if your working life has been tolerable or, better still, enjoyable and fulfilling, calling it a day can come with mixed emotions.

We’ve all come across energetic retirees with a bucket list as long as your arm, but not everyone views this pivot in their lives in the same light. Worries about health, having enough money to live on or caring for others can peak around this time.

And there’s always the potential for family friction if adult children assume that their recently retired parent has nothing else to do but look after their grandchildren.

Retirement is a huge change for the retiree but it also triggers upheaval for the whole family, especially for a partner used to having the house to themselves for most of the day. Suddenly having to share 24/7 with someone who mopes around the place or has no interests or hobbies can be a huge strain. It is a possible explanation for a spike in separations among those in their 60s.

In an ideal world, those nearing retirement age would begin planning ahead. A good place to start is by sorting out your immediate finances. (Your pension is whole a different ball game that needs to be dealt with separately.)

Once retired, you may have less money to spend day to day which makes it important to decide what your financial priorities are. Do you want to spend your money on travel, on your home or hobbies or helping out the family?

Incomes typically fall post-retirement so while you are still bringing in a regular wage it is worth dealing with outstanding debts such as loans and credit cards.

If you have multiple loans and/or several credit cards with outstanding balances, try to pay off what you can before you retire and consider consolidation to save on fees and card and interest charges.

Some people like to have two credit cards for emergencies. However, it is best to stick to one as your main card for buying and become vigilant about paying off the balance each month, bearing in mind that there will be no monthly salary to cover the cost if you overspend or let the interest build up.

Check with your bank if they offer any perks to older customers, such an account with reduced fees and charges. These accounts are usually available for those aged 66 or over.

Some banks also offer financial advice and planning for older customers but, like a lot of things in life, if you want it you have to ask for it.

Retirement can be an opportunity to reinvent yourself and to do the things you’ve always wanted to do. It can also provide more time for grandchildren which can be good or not so good depending on the circumstances.

The sentiment often expressed by grandparents is that while they love their grandchildren, it’s great to be able to hand them back to their parents. That is something that has become a lot trickier with childcare costs and places at a premium.

As a consequence, some adult children expect parents to step up for child-minding duties. Declining to do so or putting conditions in place can go down badly at times. These are potentially troubled waters so it may be worth thinking about how much babysitting you want to do and to be clear in your own mind about the boundaries before the time arrives.

Otherwise what starts out as a casual or stopgap arrangement can morph into a full-time commitment that is hard to get out of.

One solution is not to be permanently available. That’s where getting stuck into new hobbies or activities comes in. Volunteering, a new sport, a hobby, taking up an academic course or joining a choir or sea swimming group are all sociable ways of spending time that help foster good mental health and maintain the interpersonal connections that inevitably diminish when you’re no longer in full-time employment.

One often hears retirees opining that they’d prefer to watch paint drying than going hillwalking or playing bridge. But there are many other options if you dig a little. For example, rug tufting (very satisfactory as you do it with a gun and the pieces take shape fast) or joining a percussion group. Rhythm and beat are very therapeutic, and percussion includes a myriad of styles from African djembe to Japanese style drumming to learning to play the bodhrán.

Making stained glass pieces seems to suit those who like precision and wielding a soldering iron, while fused glass is a wide-open form of expression where creativity can run wild. Add to that activities like stone cutting, willow sculpture, axe throwing and Mahjong, and you are still only scratching the surface of what’s out there.

Health

Having ticked the boxes marked “money” and “filling time”, the third pillar is health and what you should do to mind it.

There is no shortage of health gurus telling us how to eat and how to exercise and it can be easy to get overwhelmed by all the noise. But strip it back and it’s pretty simple.

Move as much as possible, stay hydrated to avoid urinary tract infections, maintain social contacts and eat to preserve muscle strength, bone density and a good gut microbiome. Appetite can reduce with age so it’s important to keep a steady calorie intake to maintain energy levels and feel well.

As we get older, the combination of underlying medical conditions and natural ageing can disrupt the systems that normally keep us upright. Balance problems are one of the main fall risks for older adults.

A bad fall can be life changing which is why it’s worth incorporating exercises to maintain balance into your daily routine. These exercises require no special equipment and even 10 minutes a day has been shown to cut the risk of a fall. One of the simplest is calf raises which can be done at the worktop while you’re waiting for the kettle to boil.

ExWell Medical is a not for profit social enterprise that runs medically supervised exercise classes (and online health information sessions) for older people in the community. It was started by Dr Noel McCaffrey in 2019 and the aim is to keep people moving even if they are living with health issues, debilitating conditions or recovering from serious illnesses such as cardiac events or cancer.

The classes are pitched at different fitness levels and some can be done seated. To join a group, you must be referred by a medical practitioner. Full details of the locations of ExWell’s classes are on the organisation’s website.

For those who feel they would benefit from a more formal introduction to what retirement may bring, the Retirement Planning Council of Ireland runs year-round courses for those coming up to retirement. You can pay up and go as a private individual or your company may be willing to foot the bill so it’s worth checking that with HR.

The courses cover areas such as financial readiness, pensions, legal and lifestyle transitions.

You can contact us at OnTheMoney@irishtimes.com with personal finance questions you would like to see us address. If you missed last week’s newsletter, you can read it here.

]]>Daniel Balakov<![CDATA[Greenhushing banks quieter on climate, but letting money talk ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/environment/climate-crisis/2026/11/13/greenhushing-banks-quieter-on-climate-but-letting-money-talk/https://www.irishtimes.com/environment/climate-crisis/2026/11/13/greenhushing-banks-quieter-on-climate-but-letting-money-talk/Fri, 13 Nov 2026 14:17:39 +0000“Greenhushing” has replaced greenwashing in corporate climate action, the head of the country’s largest banks has said.

Greenhushing refers to companies deliberately downplaying or remaining silent about environmental actions, even when they are genuine

AIB chief executive Colin Hunt said many banks and businesses were talking less about climate because of political changes but were actually doing more.

“Businesses were far louder about this topic before January 2025 [when Donald Trump began his second term as US president],” he said.

“The fact of the matter is that in certain geographies people have stopped talking about transition and talking about the renewable energy opportunity, but the capital has been deployed at a pace that has never happened before.

“So we’ve moved from greenwashing to greenhushing. Nobody’s talking about it, but the critical thing is, don’t mind the talk, don’t mind the chat – is the capital being deployed?

The pioneering Somali tuk-tuk driver seeking support for a revolutionary idea at Cop31

“The answer is yes, it is and it’s being deployed largely silently.”

Hunt, who is attending the Cop31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, was speaking as AIB announced a doubling of its green finance fund for 2030.

The company set a target in 2019 of lending €30 billion to green, energy-efficient and energy transition projects by 2030. It has already loaned €28 billion.

It has now set a target of €60 billion for 2030. The money is lent to a wide range of projects from retrofits under the low-interest home energy upgrade loan scheme and green mortgages to wind and solar projects valued at hundreds of millions of euros.

Hunt said this would be a floor rather than a ceiling and demand could well outstrip the target again.

He also said AIB was still committed to green lending making up 70 per cent of all new loans issued by the bank by 2030.

“In the first three-quarters of this year, 43 per cent of our lending was green or transition in nature. We’ve got a very strong line of visibility now well into the 60 per cent and with a fair wind we will hit a target in 2030 that looked audaciously ambitious when we set it in 2019.”

During the Cop31 meeting, Hunt met former US vice-president Al Gore, who will be guest speaker at the bank’s annual sustainability conference in Dublin next February.

Hunt said Democrat victories in the US midterm elections could mean less need for greenhushing.

Climate crisis: Everything you need to know

“It might change the volume of the conversation, but the transition is happening. It is happening in front of our eyes; it’s just that people aren’t talking about it,” he said.

He said when it came to overseas loans for large renewable energy projects, the US was the fastest-growing market for AIB.

“I get a sense out of this Cop that I think there’s more optimism out there than I’ve detected in the past,” he said.

]]>Adam Vaughan<![CDATA[Microsoft outage: what happened and when will it be fixed?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/13/microsoft-outage-what-happened-and-when-will-it-be-fixed/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/13/microsoft-outage-what-happened-and-when-will-it-be-fixed/Fri, 13 Nov 2026 08:24:12 +0000Potentially millions of people were unable to access their emails, Teams chats or meetings on Thursday night and Friday morning after a Microsoft 365 outage brought down services across the globe.

The incident affected businesses, government agencies, and even Microsoft employees who were unable to email during the more than nine hours of downtime.

What happened and why – and what does it say about online services in 2026?

What happened with Microsoft?

At around 6pm on Thursday, outage website Down Detector showed a spike in users reporting issues with Microsoft 365 – the suite of cloud software that includes Teams, Word Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook. There were nearly 130,000 reports at the time.

The outage has lasted for more than 12 hours at the time of reporting, with Microsoft working to bring services back online.

What caused the Microsoft outage?

So far, the problem appears to be a configuration update which has resulted in some servers becoming overloaded and taken offline, Microsoft indicated.

When the company attempted to apply a fix, servers that had come back online again became unresponsive when traffic began returning to them.

As some servers went down, traffic was funnelled on to the remaining servers, causing traffic issues for those remaining online.

To understand what was bringing down the servers, the company began limiting the traffic that could reach affected servers in specific locations, and, on some servers, rolled back to an earlier software configuration to see if it fixed the problem.

As of 2am Friday UTC, Microsoft had narrowed down most of the issues to Microsoft Exchange – the email service behind Outlook. Teams meetings and chats had returned to service.

Why has Microsoft 365 been down for so long?

An outage that runs for more than nine hours for a service as critical as Microsoft 365 is unusual. The company has not said why it has lasted so long, but a clue might be in its updates: as servers returned to being unresponsive after being fixed, engineers had to work through alternative solutions, taking longer than expected to get servers back up and running.

Who was affected by the Microsoft outage?

Many people who rely on Microsoft 365 were reporting being unable to access their in boxes on Friday morning – where the outage has so far had the most impact.

Councils, state and government agencies, courts and schools across the globe have been among those telling the public that they are not contactable by email on Friday morning.

Businesses and healthcare services that rely on Microsoft 365 for communications were also reporting issues but said their own services remained operational.

Was the Microsoft outage a cyberattack?

Given the recent OpenAI agent attack on Medicare, and the spate of cyberattacks in Europe bringing down internet-connected fridges, some quickly guessed the global outage might be a new attack on critical infrastructure. Microsoft quickly hosed down the idea, saying there was no indication it was a cyberattack.

Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by issues with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running. ]]>Julia Demaree Nikhinson<![CDATA[Public sector pay deal: did the Government capitulate or did unions settle for too little?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/13/public-sector-pay-deal-did-the-government-capitulate-or-did-unions-settle-for-too-little/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/13/public-sector-pay-deal-did-the-government-capitulate-or-did-unions-settle-for-too-little/Fri, 13 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000There was always going to be a deal. The question was where both sides would settle. We got the answer in the early hours of Wednesday morning.

A 10.75 per cent pay hike spread out over 33 months (to March 2029) at a cost of €5.2 billion to the exchequer.

The latest round of public sector pay negotiations was unusually fraught by Irish standards but not by European standards, where industrial relations have been souring for months on the back of persistent inflation.

A fierce standoff over cost of living and pension reform has paralysed France.

If you believe one side of the commentariat, the Government capitulated at the last minute to avoid the mayhem of another one-day national strike coinciding with Ireland’s hosting of the EU summit.

But to evaluate the true merits of the deal, you need to go back to the starting point for negotiations.

Government and unions held exploratory talks in early July, but the real discussions didn’t start until October under the auspices of the Workplace Relations Commission.

On the table was the Central Bank’s latest quarterly bulletin, published the previous month, containing the bank’s inflation forecasts for 2026, 2027 and 2028 (3.4 per cent; 3.1 per cent; 2 per cent).

The forecast for 2027 had been upgraded by nearly half a percentage point since the summer, reflecting the deteriorating economic backdrop.

Public sector pay deal: What’s in it for me?

Inflation-proofing wages was the primary objective of unions.

As the negotiations progressed, the Central Bank’s inflation forecasts began to look shaky.

Oil prices were on the march again. Speculation was rife that the US and Israel were about to attack Iran again.

Unions began coming up with their own estimates of future price growth based on the latest readouts. The fear was that they would sign up to pay rises that would later be crushed by inflation.

The Government’s initial offer of a cumulative 7.75 per cent pay hike didn’t even cover the conservative inflation forecasts, hence the deadlock.

The deal eventually struck gives public sector workers in higher-income brackets a pay bump of 4.6 per cent next year (when the backdated element is included), followed by 3.1 per cent in 2028 and 3.2 per cent in 2029. Lower-paid workers, those earning less than €50,000, will get bigger pay increases.

Based on the current inflationary outlook, which has improved since the US midterm elections, this will give public sector workers modest but real wage increases.

Another benchmark for both sides to consider was the expected rise in wages in the private sector.

The Government’s recent economic and fiscal outlook, published alongside last month’s budget, forecasts that wages across the economy – which is mainly private sector – would rise by 4.1 per cent in 2027 and by 3.7 per cent in 2028 and 2029. The public sector deal is roughly comparable.

The deal includes a review clause that can be triggered by either side if economic conditions or inflation rates change “significantly”, reflecting the fact that both unions and Government are unsure about the economic outlook. Not an unreasonable position given the last five years.

Jack Chambers warns public sector pay deal could be reviewed if economy contracts

The Government typically defends pay deals as a means of preventing industrial unrest, ensuring continuity of service and pay predictability.

There is, however, a big unknown for Government.

The Department of Finance’s latest expenditure outlook report says Budget 2027 includes “the costs associated with the recruitment of circa 7,000 additional [public sector] staff”.

But public sector employment has grown by 85,000 since 2019, which equates to an average of 12,000 a year.

There is also nothing in the report or other reports about the additional staff (nurses, teachers, gardaí) needed or expected after 2027.

The Government’s €5.2 billion costing is therefore something of a shot in the dark.

In its back pocket, however, is the promise of more corporation tax, the exchequer’s golden goose. Receipts from the business tax are expected to climb to €45 billion by 2030.

But weaving more day-to-day spending around risky tax receipts is a gamble the Government has been repeatedly advised against.

The Irish Times view on the public pay deal: the Government pays up for peace

The draft deal (it still has to be ratified by unions) will cost the Government an estimated €2 billion next year, which means Budget 2027, which allocates €1.2 billion for the deal, is already out of date. €800 million out of date.

They say the definition of a good deal is when both sides walk away thinking they could have done better. That’s probably not the case here.

Both sides will sell it as a good deal in the context of the economic backdrop. But there are big unknowns to do with inflation and cost.

]]>Dara Mac Donaill<![CDATA[‘A high, then a crushing low’: Life as a start-up founder trying to get off the ground]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/13/a-high-then-a-crushing-low-life-as-a-start-up-founder-trying-to-get-off-the-ground/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/13/a-high-then-a-crushing-low-life-as-a-start-up-founder-trying-to-get-off-the-ground/Fri, 13 Nov 2026 05:55:00 +0000“We’ve had so many ups and downs,” says Eoin Everard, a healthtech start-up founder. “It’s been a long journey, but I think we’re here now.”

]]>Chris Maddaloni<![CDATA[Irish reunification will be costly - here are the key decisions which will decide the size of the bill]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/12/the-key-political-choices-that-will-determine-the-cost-of-irish-reunification/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/12/the-key-political-choices-that-will-determine-the-cost-of-irish-reunification/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 14:41:03 +0000The economics of a united Ireland has been a disputed territory for years, with analysis ranging from claims of large gains to significant costs. How do we make sense of this?

A new analysis from Prof Stephen Kinsella of the University of Limerick – The Economics of Reunification – published by Fine Gael as part of its ardfheis initiative on the topic, provides a vital guide through the arguments.

It shows, above all, two things. One is that the costs depend crucially on what model is chosen, how it is implemented and crucial negotiations with the UK on the issue of pensions and debt. And second, that the long-term growth performance of Northern Ireland will be crucial in determining the economics of reunification and whether it can be financed.

There is no one answer to the question of what a united Ireland would cost. It all depends. And this underlines the vital role of planning and preparation.

Kinsella, who is an adviser to Tánaiste Simon Harris, draws on a range of previous work, much of it undertaken post-Brexit. He estimates that the first-year cost of reunification ranges from about €3 billion to €25 billion.

This is obviously a huge range. But this is where the story lies. As the assumptions and political choices change, so do the potential costs.

Kinsella frames the issue of the economics of the reunification debate around two questions. The first is who should pay which parts of the difference between Northern Ireland’s income and its expenditure. The second is what structures can be put in place to improve convergence between income and productivity levels in Northern Ireland and the Republic.

Disposable income per household is 13 per cent higher south of the Border, and the FDI model has boosted the Republic’s economy and its public finances. In contrast, the North has a net fiscal deficit of €17 billion, funded by the UK exchequer. This does not transfer automatically to the costs of reunification, but it is important nonetheless.

In a best-case scenario, if the UK agreed to take on the historic cost of the North’s pensions bill and the debt interest on the part of the UK’s national debt which would be attributed to Northern Ireland, then much of the €17 billion deficit would fall away.

Kinsella assumes some additional costs would accrue to the Republic from investment and running a separate administration if a federal model was chosen. This is one of a range of integration models in the paper, which also includes what he calls a “managed integration” plan – involving phased harmonisation in areas such as pay and welfare rates over 15 years – and a costly scenario that harmonises everything at once.

This variety of political decisions on what form unification would take and who picks up various bills leaves a potential matrix of costs not only, of course, in year one but for many years into the future. Bringing public pay and welfare rates in the North up to the Republic’s level, for example, would be a hugely expensive exercise.

The most important decisions are:

The pensions and debt issue

What happens to the accrued pension liabilities of Northern Ireland public servants and those who qualify for a state pension has been a key difference over the years between those taking an optimistic and pessimistic view of the economic benefits of reunification. Added to this is the interest on the part of the UK national debt, allocated to Northern Ireland in relation to its size within the UK.

Together these sum to close to €10 billion of the €17 billion annual UK estimate of the Northern Ireland deficit.

Pay convergence

Partly relying on what model of unification is chosen, it is clear that, as Kinsella puts it, “a nurse, teacher or civil servant in Belfast would expect the same pay as one in Dublin and a pensioner or jobseeker in Derry would expect the same weekly payment as one in Cork.” This would cost between €2.3 billion and €12.4 billion on day one, depending on how the gaps are measured, according to the report.

Northern envy at Republic pay rates

Huge decisions would lie ahead in this area and on the wider issue of how – or whether – public services would be integrated. Savings might be expected here from unified structures, but this would mean job losses, and Kinsella warns that the gains might be modest enough.

The model chosen

Choosing between the different possible models for reunification also has an impact on the economics.

A key message is that trying to unite the two economies in an unplanned rush is potentially very expensive and would require strong growth in Northern Ireland to make the finances add up in any fashion.

So-called managed integration over 15 years would still carry a high cost, on his calculations. Extra investment needed to increase productivity in the North would also need to be factored in.

As Kinsella says in his conclusions, a key message is that political choices will drive the cost of reunification – “the price depends far more on decisions made by policymakers than on any fixed bill”. The pensions and debt issues are vital in the short term, while over time closing the pay and welfare gap is crucial.

In any scenario, the financing is complicated, requiring significant borrowing even if there is financial assistance from the UK or even the European Union (where other member states might look askance at the idea given the public-finance constraints they face).

For the financing to work, growth becomes vital. Northern Ireland has averaged 1.3 per cent a year GDP growth since the early 2000s. Under a managed transition scenario, this would need to rise – depending on the assumptions – to between 3 per cent and 4.7 per cent on average each year to underpin a funding model.

Kinsella concludes that “this is a high bar, but it is possible”. Other assumptions might lower the growth targets a bit – again showing the importance of the key decisions.

A key conclusion from reading the report is that the potential financial implications for the Republic and its citizens are significant. Kinsella points to a range of potential costs per head in the Republic, which runs from €650 in year one to more than €2,600, with ongoing significant costs in future years.

Cross-Border tax rules putting off employers and workers, says report

Ireland’s public finances give it leeway to fund reunification, but this still carries costs. “However the costs are shared,” Kinsella writes, “someone has to pay them year by year.”

Like previous work by economists John FitzGerald and Edgar Morgenroth, the report points to the investment needs of Northern Ireland in areas such as education and skills, infrastructure and other measures to boost productivity.

There are potential gains from unification, too, as – for example – corporate taxes are cut in the North, encouraging inward investment, and new trade opportunities open up as the Irish Border disappears and Northern Ireland becomes a full part of the EU.

The extent of the resulting dynamic is hugely difficult to model with any confidence, but the North’s lacklustre economic performance compared with the Republic does point to some potential gains.

As the report concludes, whether reunification happens is a political and constitutional question. But the economics will be vital, and the report again underlines the complexity of the task and the huge preparations which would be required.

]]>Bill_Vorasate<![CDATA[Panic over cyberattacks plays straight into the hands of those behind them]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/12/panic-over-cyberattacks-plays-into-hands-of-those-behind-them/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/12/panic-over-cyberattacks-plays-into-hands-of-those-behind-them/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000Put the kettle on. Right now, everyone would benefit from sitting down and taking a few minutes to have a cup of something.

My weekend was largely spent calming people down after last week’s cyberattacks. Supermarket fridges got hacked, there were bomb threats to airlines and the week ended with several media organisations being evacuated due to more bomb threats.

Plenty of otherwise rational people took this as a reason for all-out panic and as a sign of the need to prepare for the end of time. Civilisation isn’t about to collapse and it’s time you had that cuppa.

All of the recent attacks or threats were designed to disrupt. That is in keeping with the experience of countries that previously held the presidency of the Council of the EU.

There was certainly some fiscal impact but the core goal was to cause disorder. Some stock was lost from fridges, some flights were rescheduled and David McCullagh regretted not grabbing his jumper.

Many people became preoccupied with thoughts of, “if the hackers could do this, then what else are they capable of?”.

That’s the wrong question to ask. They are capable of far worse, but you should be asking if doing so is really in their interest.

The big fear I kept hearing about was a national blackout. At their operational best, the most sophisticated hackers could knock out power in Ireland for about 12 hours. Weather is a far more powerful and probable threat to the grid than any malicious actor.

The goal of these disruptions, which are almost always caused by state-backed actors, is to cause fear. It may be Russia today, North Korea tomorrow or the Federated States of Micronesia at the weekend. Instilling fear and uncertainty is a key part of the package.

It probably doesn’t help that these attacks are usually backed up by disinformation campaigns. We need only look at how effective Russia’s disinformation campaign in Poland has been in damaging public support there for Ukraine to see how effective this can be.

The playbook is awfully similar to what we’re seeing here. Some legitimate concerns – which we have had in Ireland following these attacks – are exaggerated to exacerbate fear.

Having a range of goals also works in favour of cybercriminals. Some want to disrupt, some want to stoke fear, others want to steal information or money and quite a few have a cocktail involving elements of all of these. Variety of motive makes it tougher to defend as the method of attack will vary.

No matter what the goal is, it is most unlikely that an all-out attack on Ireland’s core systems is uppermost in the mind of any attackers. The truth is that it does not make sense on a cost-benefit analysis to engage in something at that level.

Attacking the fridges was a good test to see what could be done. Using anonymous accounts to spread bomb threats en masse was a low-to-no-cost means of causing disruption. Taking out the grid or worse? That involves a real commitment and potential blowback. Not from Ireland, oh no, but from those outside Ireland who would be irked.

Multinational data centres and other tech infrastructure here make for tasty targets. Attacking one or a few is certainly a reasonably likely scenario that state-backed cyber attackers will consider. Going for a true shutdown? That gets the Americans angry because it disrupts their businesses. The US government is more than capable of striking back in kind.

Ukraine blowing up three Yandex data centres caused chaos in Moscow. Cyber retaliation by the US government to a cyberattack on their tech giants would make that look like a nosebleed.

Even if the US threat wasn’t there, while Ireland may punch above its weight for its population and economy size, we are far from the juiciest target in the EU, let alone globally.

Besides, with far less risk and at far lower cost, those who caused chaos with our fridges, flights and media last week can get a great return on investment.

They have already got plenty of people afraid. People are fretting about what they might need to do for an improbable attack. Many are realising that they aren’t really capable personally of doing much about it if anything did happen.

Having a torch or a charged power bank is sensible at the best of times. As I said earlier, weather is a real threat to power in this State and winter is coming.

There comes a point where obsessing over being ready for a threat you cannot do much about becomes unhealthy. It doesn’t take long for many people to hit that point.

Between two decades of covering cybersecurity and a lifelong interest in dystopian fiction, I’ve done my share of thinking about worst-case scenarios. Dying carefree beats the hell out of living in fear.

Yes, Ireland had a few mad days of it. It’ll have a few more wild ones in the days and weeks to come but UCD got promoted to football’s top domestic tier and you’ve made yourself a cuppa. Enjoy the good things and relax.

A. Transferring the property in a part-gift, part-loan arrangement works legally, but it may not be the most tax efficient option, says Carl Donnelly, head of tax at accountancy firm Cronin.

“You may end up paying more in total tax than if you made an outright gift,” says Donnelly.

In transferring the property to his son, the father will be liable for capital gains tax (CGT) as though he were selling it at its full market value of €490,000. This is regardless of whether the transfer is, in part, structured as a loan, says Donnelly.

“CGT of 31 per cent is due on your whole gain, whether you make an outright gift or a part-gift,” he says.

The father is right. The law will let him use the CGT he owes as a credit against any capital acquisitions tax (CAT) arising for the son. This is because both taxes arise on the same event and the same property, says Donnelly.

A part-gift still qualifies for this offset. However, Revenue practice is to only give credit for the share of the CGT that relates to the gift element – €200,000 in this case.

“That amounts to 200/490ths of the CGT he owes on the property,” says Donnelly.

Also, the credit cannot be more than the CAT the son might owe on the “gifted” element of the property, says Donnelly.

A child can receive up to €420,000 tax-free from his parents before CAT of 33 per cent kicks in. This threshold is cumulative, so it is reduced by any earlier gifts or inheritances from either parent.

“The father’s CGT bill stays the same.”

Gift the property outright instead, and the son would have received €67,000 over this tax-free threshold, factoring in the annual small gift exemption of €3,000.

If the loan is interest-free, the interest the son would otherwise pay also counts as a gift to him each year, although the €3,000 annual gift exemption may cover it, he says.

MedWrite has a distributed team of 18 split between Ireland and the Middle East.

“A significant part of the investment to date has gone into AI research and development, building our data science and engineering capability and validating how the technology performs in real clinical settings. This has included clinical studies with Irish hospitals examining the accuracy, safety and time savings delivered by the technology,” Kirwan says. “We have also invested heavily in the software around the AI, building the MedWrite platform across web, mobile and desktop and integrating it into the systems hospitals already use.

“The third major area has been security, clinical governance and regulatory compliance,” he adds. “Healthcare has a very high bar for introducing new technology, particularly technology handling patient information, so we have built those requirements into the MedWrite platform from the outset.”

]]><![CDATA[European shares hit record as AI optimism returns]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/11/european-shares-hit-record-as-ai-optimism-returns/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/11/european-shares-hit-record-as-ai-optimism-returns/Wed, 11 Nov 2026 19:49:30 +0000European stocks set a fresh record on Wednesday, buoyed by rebounding energy and tech shares.

The performance came following upbeat forecasts from Siemens Energy, while investor confidence in artificial intelligence showed signs of returning after positive results at US-based AI cloud computing firm CoreWeave.

The neocloud company saw its shares rally by more than 25 per cent in early trading, which left it on track for its best day of trading since June.

Dublin

The Iseq All-Share Index rose marginally by 0.6 per cent to close at 15,035.08 on Wednesday.

Kingspan, which forecast a spike in 2026 trading profit earlier this week, saw its share price rise to €99 on Tuesday before it fell back to a low of around €92 per share. On Wednesday, it was one of the biggest gainers of the day, as its stock rose to €98.70, up 1.44 per cent since open.

Greencoat Renewables, which last week reported a €11.9 million profit for the first half of the year, was the biggest riser of the day as it added 2.1 per cent to close at €0.82. Kerry Group also registered a gain of near 2 per cent, as its price rose to €99.25.

Iseq-heavyweight Ryanair traded down nearly 2.5 per cent to €26 per share. Last week, the firm reported higher revenues, but profits were lower during the first half of its financial year to the end of September.

Insurance company FBD Holdings fell 2 per cent, while home builder Cairn Homes’ share price was down 3 per cent since open to €2.75.

London

The London stock market closed higher, with the FTSE 100 Index up almost 0.8 per cent at 10,835. The performance on Wednesday means the index is rising towards its record high.

Computer services company Computacenter, up by close to 3.9 per cent, was one of the top risers of the day, followed by investment group Polar Capital, which gained 4.7 per cent.

Rising oil and metals prices also contributed to the gains of the day in London, with BP’s share price up 2.7 per cent, while Shell rose 1.3 per cent.

Mining firms were also among the strong performers, as Antofagasta and Glencore were each up by more than 2 per cent.

British media company ITV slipped 3.6 per cent after warning that fourth-quarter advertising revenue could decline by up to 10 per cent.

Government wants to use pay deal to drive digital transformation

Europe

The Stoxx Europe 600 Index rose 0.7 per cent to close at 663.05 on Wednesday, surpassing its previous record closing high set in August.

Siemens Energy AG rose as much as 10 per cent after the company said profit margins will swell to as much as 22 per cent by 2030. It said the rise would be driven by booming demand for gas turbines and power-grid equipment.

Shares of its peers Schneider Electric and Legrand gained 3 per cent and 2.2 per cent, respectively.

Elsewhere, Czech defence group CSG NV fell 21 per cent to an all-time low after the firm reported revenue that missed estimates and lowered its full-year profit margin outlook.

New York

In the past week, the tech-heavy Nasdaq was hit heavily as investors showed concern over what a Democratic sweep of Congress would mean for the AI sector.

On Wednesday, US stocks extended gains as the technology-heavy Nasdaq 100 briefly erased losses suffered in the aftermath of the US midterm elections.

In early afternoon trading in New York, the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 0.3 per cent, the S&P 500 was 1.5 per cent higher and the Nasdaq rose 2 per cent.

The gains on Wednesday have come following better-than-expected results from CoreWeave, excitement over Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) and a blockbuster quarter for OpenAI.

CoreWeave’s rise came after the cloud infrastructure firm announced better-than-anticipated revenue and a full-year outlook that came in stronger than Wall Street expected after the market closed on Tuesday.

Shares in Nvidia rose by almost 4 per cent after shedding about $430 billion (€387 billion) in the previous two sessions.

On Wednesday, the Financial Times reported the company’s board has hired former New York federal prosecutor Joon H Kim to conduct its internal probe into chief executive Jensen Huang’s alleged relationship with a woman the US intelligence believe was working as a spy for China.

Oil rebounded following two consecutive days of losses, with Brent rising back above $93 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate trading near $88 a barrel.

US voters have rejected data centres and AI. What happens now?

]]><![CDATA[Web Summit a washout as attendees count the cost of unused €1,595 tickets]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/11/as-heavy-rain-lashes-lisbon-web-summits-wednesday-schedule-is-washed-away/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/11/as-heavy-rain-lashes-lisbon-web-summits-wednesday-schedule-is-washed-away/Wed, 11 Nov 2026 16:33:37 +0000If the heavy rain and strong winds were not clear enough indicators that Web Summit’s Wednesday offering had been washed off, the sight of half a dozen men taking down the front gates settled the matter for those who still turned up at the Lisbon venue.

The eerily quiet industrial suburbs in the Portuguese capital’s eastern area told their own story. The all-but silent road leading to the arena was interrupted only by the small team of security guards sheltering from the rain, occasionally redirecting hopefuls away.

A small crowd of German- and Polish-speaking men appeared at the would-be entrance shortly before 10am, but soon accepted defeat.

With general admission tickets costing €1,595 and VIPs priced up to €1,950 – not to mention the rare “chairperson” ticketholder who forked out €25,000 – who could really blame them for trying to get their money’s worth?

The schedule of events on Wednesday was cancelled on Tuesday afternoon following earlier comments from Lisbon’s mayor, who said “everything indicates” it could not function. The Portuguese prime minister went further, issuing a recommendation to suspend the day’s events.

The country braced for a day in which two storms overlapped, with the southern half of Portugal (including Lisbon) under level-red warnings for extreme weather.

But not all hope was lost. A saving grace came shortly after 11.30am on Wednesday. “Web Summit is back tomorrow” was the title of the email, sent by the organisers of the technology conference to all its ticket holders.

Web Summit cancels events as Portugal issues ‘state of alert’ amid storm warnings

“It will be the busiest Thursday ever, with more speakers and more meetups than ever before – with many rescheduled from Wednesday,” the email read. Attendees were encouraged to “keep an eye on the schedule later today for updates”.

Only 20 minutes beforehand, Web Summit chief executive Paddy Cosgrave broke the news to the organisation’s Slack channel. In written correspondence, he said the production team had “worked through the night until 3am to make the site safe”, adding that they would do so again on Wednesday night so “it is perfect for first thing tomorrow morning”.

“Literal heroes,” he wrote, prompting replies that included about 150 praying emojis, 110 red hearts, 90 clapping hands and 12 crowns.

With the nation under a state of alert, a hush of inactivity swept the capital city for much of the day – interrupted only by the odd public bus continuing to service its route, often driving through large puddles and splashing upon empty pavements.

Saldanha is an upmarket area in the central suburbs that serves as Lisbon’s big business hub while also keeping a posh neighbourhood feel. This is a spot so popular with Web Summit visitors that its metro stop required a heightened police presence on the platforms to ensure order during the morning rush to the conference.

At Web Summit opener, Palestine gets a brief mention and the loudest cheer

On Wednesday, it was a ghost town, with only two people on its platform, waiting for the metro’s red line that terminates at the airport. They were both carrying suitcases. A couple, who appeared to be lost tourists, emerged from the elevator. They looked utterly confused and quickly left again.

The Vasco da Gama shopping centre (already decorated for Christmas), was a shell of its usual self. Once used as a throughway from the Oriente metro stop to Web Summit’s front gates, it was a slow-moving ocean of thousands on Tuesday morning. Only a day later, neither a tech bro nor a high-street shopper could get their fix.

Cosgrave and his Web Summit team will be hoping it’s business as usual on Thursday, the final day of the annual conference.

]]>Filipe Amorim<![CDATA[Provisional liquidators appointed to Dublin-registered Fly4 due to Iran war fuel hikes]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/11/provisional-liquidators-appointed-to-dublin-registered-airline-hit-by-iran-war-fuel-hikes/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/11/provisional-liquidators-appointed-to-dublin-registered-airline-hit-by-iran-war-fuel-hikes/Wed, 11 Nov 2026 17:09:07 +0000The High Court has appointed joint provisional liquidators to a Dublin-registered charter airline which has run into financial difficulties due to the Iran war and the rise in the price of fuel.

Fly4 Airlines Green Ltd, with registered office at Dublin Airport, was set up just over three years ago in August 2023 as a joint venture between Polish airline Enter Air and TUI B, part of the German tourism and travel group TUI.

On Tuesday, Bernard Dunleavy, counsel for Fly4 with Barry Mansfield, said the board had decided to apply to appoint provisional liquidators in an effort to deal with an insolvency situation which will arise at the end of the month and in a situation where valuable leased aircraft are located around Europe and need to be repatriated.

Judge Brian Cregan said he was satisfied to appoint Mark Degnan and Brendan O’Reilly of Interpath as joint provisional liquidators.

Douglas Fay, Fly4 chief financial officer and director, said in written evidence that the appointment of the provisional liquidators is necessary because the company considers its assets and property are exposed to immediate and substantial risk.

It has four Boeing 737-800s, all under lease arrangements and located in Turkey, Germany and Belgium.

Fay said the lease provisions are significant because an insolvency event may trigger rights in favour of the relevant lessors to repossess the aircraft or require their return. The company may also remain exposed to maintenance, return-condition and indemnity liabilities.

Fly4 began trading in about August 2023 and in 2024 its financial performance included significant start-up costs of about €8 million, which consumed the capital provided by Enter Air and TUI.

Utilisation of aircraft was low during the winter of 2023/24 due to a lack of lead time and name recognition for a new brand, Fay said. This resulted in losses of some €16 million for 2024.

Performance in 2025 was much improved but continuation of low utilisation during winter meant losses of about €4 million.

The company had initially forecast 2026 would be profitable, with an expectation of €3 million in earnings, but the actual performance resulted in a loss of €1.1 million for the first nine months. Fay said the performance, which “fell materially short of expectations, was due to the impact of the US–Iran war and the increased fuel costs associated with it”.

The company has a cash balance of about €2.7 million, but underlying cash cost run-rate is €2.5 million to €3 million a month. It also expects a net exposure of some €4 million for heavy maintenance costs for the aircraft over the next six months.

The court heard the company has 12 Irish employees, eight UK employees and some 80 others are engaged by third parties as air crew.

The judge said the matter could return to court at the end of the month.

]]>Nick Bradshaw for The Irish Time<![CDATA[Ecocem’s low-carbon cement offers hope of cutting construction sector emissions]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/11/structure-built-with-new-low-carbon-cement-unveiled-at-dublin-event/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/11/structure-built-with-new-low-carbon-cement-unveiled-at-dublin-event/Wed, 11 Nov 2026 11:00:08 +0000Ecocem has developed a cement with carbon emissions that are 70 per cent below those in conventional European cement.

A consortium that also includes home builder Cairn Homes, concrete supplier Kilsaran and University College Dublin (UCD), unveiled a “scale demonstrator” of the new low-carbon technology on Wednesday.

The two-storey stand-alone structure was put on display at Cairn’s innovation hub at Seven Mills in Dublin 22.

Ecocem developed its low-clinker cement technology over more than 10 years at its research and innovation centre near Paris. Clinker is the main ingredient in traditional cement.

The new product has been shown to deliver up to 70 per cent lower carbon dioxide emissions than conventional European cement “while integrating with existing cement manufacturing, concrete production and construction processes,” the consortium said.

“Importantly, it has been designed to be cost-competitive with conventional cement and does not carry a green premium,” it said.

Traditional cement accounts for 7-8 per cent of global carbon emissions.

Ecocem, in partnership with French company CB Green, has secured French government backing for a new €50 million advanced cement technology (ACT) production plant in Dunkirk, which is expected to be operational next year with an annual capacity of 300,000 tonnes.

The company’s low-carbon cement has already been deployed across more than 40 projects in Europe, including a 150-unit residential complex near Paris.

Initial results showed that the concrete achieved its required strength after 28 days, “as expected and that it is equal to traditional cement in terms of durability and lifespan”.

While ACT is expected to be covered in the revised European cement standard in 2027, its wider use in structural concrete in Ireland will require further regulatory clearances.

With the support of the Department of Enterprise, the National Standards Authority of Ireland is developing new regulations around cementitious binders – the materials that are used to make cement – such as ACT.

“This could provide a potential route to market for ACT in Ireland by 2028, subject to the necessary regulatory and standards approvals,” the consortium said.

Attending the event was Minister for Enterprise Peter Burke, who said: “The work being demonstrated here, using innovative low-carbon cement technology, shows how we can significantly reduce industrial emissions while continuing to deliver the homes and infrastructure both Ireland and Europe need.”

Donal O’Riain, founder and chief executive of Ecocem, said: “Ireland can deliver the homes and infrastructure it needs with significantly lower carbon emissions. This project demonstrates that the technology to rapidly and cost-effectively decarbonise cement already exists and integrates with the manufacturing and construction processes used today.”

]]>simonkr<![CDATA[Web Summit cancels events as Portugal issues ‘state of alert’ amid storm warnings]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/everything-indicates-web-summit-will-be-called-off-tomorrow-says-lisbon-mayor/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/everything-indicates-web-summit-will-be-called-off-tomorrow-says-lisbon-mayor/Tue, 10 Nov 2026 20:29:13 +0000Web Summit, the Irish-founded technology conference that has brought some 70,000 people to Lisbon this week, has cancelled its events organised to take place on Wednesday as Portugal is placed under a “state of alert” in advance of extreme weather conditions.

The company confirmed the decision shortly after 7.30pm Tuesday evening, following hours of speculation prompted by the mayor of Lisbon saying “everything indicates that Web Summit will not be able to function tomorrow”.

An hour beforehand, the prime minister of Portugal Luís Montenegro said in a press conference his office had “already issued our recommendation that the event’s activities be suspended for tomorrow”.

Montenegro said this was “for various reasons”, including “the fact that many participants are foreigners who do not have the same familiarity with emergency procedures that citizens residing in our territory naturally have”.

“The decision rests with them,” Montenegro said. “In any case, I believe that with common sense, a sense of consideration and responsibility, no one will unnecessarily expose citizens, whether national or foreign, to situations of greater risk.”

An email to Web Summit ticket holders sent at 7.38pm by the company read: “Web Summit will of course respect the Government’s direction, and accordingly, Day 2 will not take place.”

“The safety and security of our attendees, staff and contractors is always our absolute priority,” it continued, adding it “aims to proceed with Day 3 as planned, following the passing of Storm Charles.”

“We will continue to work closely with the relevant authorities and emergency services, monitor conditions and provide further updates as soon as confirmed information becomes available.”

All of Portugal has been placed under an amber warning for rainfall, with the southern half of the country, including Lisbon, under a red warning for wind, issued by the Portuguese Institute for the Sea and Atmosphere, the country’s weather authority, on Tuesday.

While the country experiences two storms, Bruna and Charles, at once with two days of overlap, the meteorological agency has forecast “periods of heavy rain and strong winds” that could “reach 120km/h and exceed 150km/h”.

Schools across the country are to be closed for the day, as the national government will place its citizens on the Iberian mainland under a 24-hour “state of alert” that mandates the suspension of outdoor events and restrictions on movement.

Web Summit organisers have had to cancel a slew of high-profile guests arranged to speak on Wednesday – among them: former president of Ireland and founding member of The Elders, Mary Robinson.

An anti-Web Summit protest, organised to take place on Wednesday evening by a grand coalition of Lisbon housing activists, has also been cancelled.

The technology conference, which was founded by businessman Paddy Cosgrave, has attracted controversy in Lisbon, with its opening ceremony having coincided with the end of a housing rights encampment protest on one of the capital’s most prominent plazas.

Lisbon mayor Carlos Moedas had ordered the 200 or so protesters to move from Rossio Square to make room for a Christmas market. The dispute made its way through the judicial system; however, demonstrators called off the action Monday night, saying they must “enlarge the movement” and “go elsewhere”.

Edward McCloskey of Irish firm WaterWipes: The target is becoming a ‘billion-dollar brand’

]]><![CDATA[Irish mortgage interest costs double in five years, with rents up 36% in same period]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/11/irish-mortgage-interest-costs-double-in-five-years-on-higher-rates-and-home-values/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/11/irish-mortgage-interest-costs-double-in-five-years-on-higher-rates-and-home-values/Wed, 11 Nov 2026 14:02:37 +0000The average Irish monthly mortgage interest bill has doubled in the five years to October, driven by higher loan rates and an ongoing surge in home values, according to the Central Statistics Office (CSO).

Mortgage interest costs are now at their highest level since October 2008, the CSO said in an occasional paper published on Wednesday highlighting developments in rents, mortgage interest payments and household maintenance costs.

The report did not give a euro value for the average household interest cost.

However, separate data published by the Central Bank on Wednesday show that the average new rate for an Irish mortgage stood at 3.52 per cent in September, which is up from 2.72 per cent in September 2021, following a net spike in Central Bank rates over the period.

Irish residential prices have jumped by 41 per cent in the five years to August, according to data contained in the CSO’s most recent monthly report on property values, published last month.

The new CSO report shows that rent prices have increased by 36 per cent over five years and are at their highest level since the agency started compiling such figures in 1996 as part of its analysis of general consumer price inflation.

Meanwhile, household maintenance costs, which includes materials and services for household repair and maintenance, have risen 19.3 per cent in the last five years, it said.

“When we look at price indices, which show price trends over time, in October 2026, mortgage interest costs were at their highest level since October 2008. This was due to a number of interest rate rises and the increasing value of houses over this time period,” the CSO said.

“Rental price levels as measured by the CPI are at their highest level since the CSO began publishing detailed sub-indices in November 1996 and have increased every month since July 2021.”

   <description>Eine große Störung hat weltweit Unternehmen und Nutzerinnen und Nutzer zentraler Cloud-Angebote des Softwarekonzerns Microsoft teilweise lahmgelegt. A Belgian court has overturned an order to seize funds from Poland’s air-traffic control agency, PANSA, as part of pharmaceutical giant Pfizer’s efforts to enforce a €1.3 billion claim for COVID-19 vaccines Poland ordered but later refused to receive and pay for.

The ruling, issued on Thursday, followed a legal challenge by PANSA to the freezing of its funds. It argued that it was not a party to the dispute between Pfizer and the Polish state.
