The post How Rhoda AI is using video data to create generalized AI models for robots appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

Rhoda pretrains its models on internet-scale video to build a strong prior on motion, physics, and physical interaction. | Source: Rhoda AI

Earlier this year, Rhoda AI emerged from 18 months of stealth with $450 million in Series A funding. The company is working with customers in automotive, manufacturing, logistics, and e-commerce to deploy its direct video action, or DVA, model for robotics.

“We’re focused on deploying in the real world, and that means you have to deal with the messiness of the real world. Every run can be different,” Jagdeep Singh, the co-founder and CEO of Rhoda AI, told The Robot Report. “Every configuration can be different, and you need a really robust model. To build a robust model, you need a massive training dataset.”

A large training dataset is exactly what allowed large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT to rapidly progress in recent years. Physical AI has trailed behind those models because the same dataset doesn’t exist for the physical world, noted Singh.

“Every word ever put on the internet, from Shakespeare to Reddit, was used to train these AI models. In the physical AI world, you didn’t have an internet-scale dataset,” he said. “People tried to collect their own data by tele-operating robots, and that approach made for interesting lab demonstrations in robots that could fold T-shirts or make coffees and so on, but none of those demonstrations were robust enough to cross over into the real world. The number of autonomous manipulation capable robots that are solving real world problems today is effectively zero.”

Rhoda AI is betting on using video to data to close this gap and to create truly generalized robotics.

How does a DVA model work?

Many physical AI developers are creating vision-language-action (VLA) models, which allow robots to learn from data from images or videos of its surroundings and text instructions. These models, however, still struggle to cope with the variability of the real world, according to Rhoda AI.

The company claimed that its DVA model, which it recently extended with mobile DVA, combines manipulation and mobility into one policy.

“The way it works is the model will look at a history of video frames and action tokens and language tokens. From that history, or from that context, it will make a prediction in video for the next few 100 milliseconds, the next half second or so,” explained Singh. “It’ll predict the scene and what it thinks will happen in that scene. Once you have that prediction, you pass it to a second part of the model, which is an action converter. It takes the video scene and spits out robot actions.”

“Once you have that action space output, you can execute those actions on a real robot. The robot then moves for that half second, and then you make a new observation, because the state of the world has changed, and you make a new prediction for the next half second,” he continued. “It’s basically making an observation, a prediction of what should happen next, a conversion to action, an execution of the action, and then you close the loop and make a new observation and a new prediction based on that new observation.”

For Rhoda AI, quantity of data is key

According to Singh, any AI model that’s trained on a small dataset is going to be very brittle. These models could work if the inference time distribution of data is very similar to the training time distribution, but as those distributions diverge, then the model starts to fail.

“Hundreds of years of videos were used to train the model, so the model has seen just an incredible diversity of everything: baseball videos, people throwing darts, waves crashing on a beach, or trees blowing in the wind,” Singh said. “Not just videos that have humans in them. Every video has something to teach the model about how the world works. Essentially, the entire internet becomes like a physics classroom.”

Rhoda AI uses video data for pretraining. “Once you’ve gotten that pretraining, you then apply a small amount of task-specific training, maybe 10 to 20 hours’ worth, similar to the way you would train a new worker on an assembly line,” said Singh. “They already come in with a certain set of skills, and you need to teach them the workflow of your particular company. With that little bit of post training, the model is able to do things that traditional robots cannot do.”

The Palo Alto, Calif.-based company aims to make a model that can understand the world generally. For this, it doesn’t limit the data it uses to just human-centric videos.

“We looked at more heavily curated videos that only had human, egocentric manipulation in them,” Singh said. “There was a question of maybe those videos were better to train on. We found that the models that perform the best were the ones actually trained on the broadest data sets, including things that were not obviously relevant to manipulation.”

This generalization also enables Rhoda AI’s models to generalize across different robot embodiments. In fact, the specific robot embodiment only comes into play in the post-training phase.

How does Rhoda AI offer its models?

Singh said Rhoda AI is a full-stack company, and it offers its technology in a range of methods.

“We always own the AI layer, that’s the core,” Singh said. “In terms of the body or hardware layer, we can run with our body or a third-party body. In terms of the skills, we can be the ones training the skills, or we can let third parties train the skills. That provides the largest set of solutions to our customers, and that’s really our mission.”

Internally, Rhoda AI is focusing on developing skills in manufacturing and logistics.

“We’re going after those areas because there’s an immediate problem there,” added Singh. “Many manufacturing and logistics companies have a shortage of labor. Many industries have been offshored for decades because its too expensive to build in those economies. So this technology offers a path to repatriate some of those industries.”

Looking ahead, Rhoda AI aims to continue getting its model out into the real world. Singh said he believes robotics’ “ChatGPT moment” will be coming sooners than people expect.

“The kind of approach we’re taking really has the potential to get us there because the only way to get that level of generality is to train on a dataset that has both the scale of the internet and diversity of the internet,” said Singh. “If you don’t have both those things, your models will not be able to generalize well enough.”

]]>

NVIDIA says it will continue to support customers amid its leadership changes. Source: NVIDIA

After a tumultuous week that saw NVIDIA Corp.’s stock drop by about 18.5%, CEO Jensen Huang has stepped down. The company today said it has appointed Collette Kress, executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO and investor Harvey C. Jones as its first board chair.

Huang, who is one of the most recognizable figures in AI, recently admitted to extramarital affairs including with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Megaspeed who is suspected of being a Chinese spy, and Kimberly Powell, vice president of healthcare at NVIDIA.

“To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” Jensen Huang wrote in a statement on Nov. 8. “Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s board of directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully.”

Huang co-founded NVIDIA in 1993, and it makes graphics processing units (GPUs) and software architectures that are the basis for much of advanced computing and AI today. The Santa Clara, Calif.-based company has a market capitalization of about $4 trillion, and its simulation and other technologies are used in industrial manipulators, autonomous mobile robots (AMRs), and emerging humanoid robots.

Kress and Jones to provide business continuity

Kress has served as EVP and CFO of NVIDIA since joining the company in September 2013. NVIDIA said that she has played a key role in its growth and evolution. Prior to joining NVIDIA, Kress spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies including Cisco and Microsoft.

“NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” stated Kress. “We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”

Jones has been an entrepreneur, technology executive, and venture investor for more than 30 years. He has served as CEO and executive chairman of Synopsys.

“Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Jones about Kress. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments, and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”

Submit your innovation now!

NVIDIA to endure competitive scrutiny

China leads the world in robotics manufacturing and usage, but it still relies on U.S. AI chips and edge computing components. Amid heightened trade conflicts, NVIDIA has worked with numerous global humanoid developers, including Unitree Robotics and Alibaba Cloud. Recent revelations about possible circumvention of U.S. export controls could lead to further investigations and reputational damage.

But in the meantime, NVIDIA has continued to support the robotics industry. Just this week, NVIDIA introduced GR00T 2, an updated open frontier world action model, and Isaac Lab 3.0, the latest version of its open-source robot learning framework. Huang spoke at GTC Berlin last month (see video below).

In September, NVIDIA said it planned to acquire Hugging Face Inc.’s open AI development platform for $12.9 billion. Pollen Robotics, a Bordeaux, France-based subsidiary of Hugging Face, had developed the Microduck open-source legged robot, which uses a Chinese processor.

NVIDIA last month described how robots such as Microduck could use its Isaac Lab learning framework, Newton physical modeling, Omniverse libraries, and Isaac Sim simulation for evaluation. Its deal with Hugging Face will receive more scrutiny, and competitors such as AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, and Intel may try to position themselves are more reliable Western suppliers.

Reuters and Monrningstar noted that Huang’s departure could slow deals around AI. The departure of a prominent tech exec could also lead to greater government scrutiny of trade deals as efforts continue to build so-called sovereign AI and robotics. The Robot Report will continue tracking these developments.

The post NVIDIA replaces CEO amid China AI and robotics concerns appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

Viam provides a software platform to ease robotics development. Source: Viam

Returning from RoboBusiness and RobOpsCon, I have never felt more optimistic about the robotics — I mean the physical AI — industry. Billion-dollar valuations and groundbreaking technology continue to outpace yesterday’s innovations at warp speed.

At the same time, too many brilliant entrepreneurs are languishing in taking their ideas from the lab to market. These startups, led by domain experts, are on a mission to automate their industries. However, they get stuck in ROS purgatory, unable to turn pilots into revenue-generating bots.

In 2020, Eliot Horowitz set out to create a better way to build and deploy smart machines. Drawing on his experience as co-founder and chief technology officer of MongoDB, Horowitz created Viam, a universal software abstraction layer for building and deploying hardware systems across enterprise fleets, or, as the company describes it, “The harness for physical AI.”

“In the past, robotics startups needed years of R&D and were faced with building a huge amount of infrastructure to make a project something more than a science experiment,” said Horowitz. “What we see with Viam is that a small team starting from zero can prototype in weeks or months, iterate, deploy, and capture real business with incredible velocity by leveraging Viam’s tools and harness for physical AI. We’re incredibly excited to be providing the ingredients needed to grow this new wave of robotics.”

The new RoboSimStudio is an open-source project that enables agentic AI coding of robotic simulation environments. | Credit: UC Berkeley

UC Berkeley and NVIDIA have released open-source tools for a new approach: enabling teams of AI coding agents to write, simulate, and refine readable robot programs.

Since the early days of industrial robots, programming, tuning, and troubleshooting robotic workcells has taken weeks to months. New research coming out of UC Berkeley has demonstrated that new agentic AI programming tools could change how industrial robots are coded and maintained.

Why is this important? As anyone who’s programmed an industrial workcell knows, implementing the code has to wait until the end of the design and fabrication process. The robot needs to be installed in the workcell; all of the feeders, conveyance, and other elements also need to be installed. The pressure to get this done all falls on the software team, often when the project deadline is looming.

The new toolset goes beyond the idea of “vibe coding” a robot application. While it generates code with large language models (LLMs), what’s novel is the use of AI agents to manage the coding, testing and deployment.

“Agentic robotics is a fundamental shift in how robots are programmed,” said Ken Goldberg, the William S. Floyd Jr. Distinguished Chair in Engineering at UC Berkeley. “Instead of collecting massive amounts of data and hand-tuning every behavior, teams of agents can quickly generate, test, and refine robot programs that allow human engineers to interpret how the programs work for fine-tuning and verification.”

Researchers introduce GaP and VABAR

  • Graph-as-Policy (GaP) is a modular framework that splits a task into skills — perception, grasp planning, collision-free motion — which agents generate, connect and rehearse in simulation.
  • Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics (VABAR) is a benchmark of six tasks: tool sorting, tool hanging, gear meshing, syringe packing, cable insertion, and cable routing. It is built built on Isaac Lab-Arena and Newton, with standardized variations and difficulty tiers.
  • The UC Berkeley and NVIDIA team presented the concept at CoRL 2026 this week in Austin, Texas.

How the toolset works

Dr. Goldberg described the research to The Robot Report. In September, Eric Chen, one of his graduate students, give GPT-6 Astra Eric’s new RoboSimStudio tool to see if it could generate not just a graphic model, but also a full 3D simulation of a scene. And that’s exactly what happened.

According to Goldberg, Chen gave the model a video and this new tool, and within an hour, it had generated a Newton simulation that was incredibly similar to the video.

“When a new frontier model came out in early September, they gave it the tool and a video,” said Goldberg. “Within about an hour, it produced a Newton simulation closely matching the video, by iterative trial and error.”

“And Newton [simulation] is really wonderful,” he added. “The problem is Newton is very complicated. It has a lot of parameters, hundreds of parameters. So generally, people didn’t really use it that much because it’s just too complicated, too many dials and switches.”

Goldberg praised Chen for pulling this together. Initially, Chen built the tool just for himself.

“I want my student Eric to get credit for this,” he said. “He basically sat down and built a new interface for Newton called RoboSimStudio. It is basically just an interface that makes you have sliders on the right-hand side of your screen, and you have a visualizer on the left. … You can tune all these parameters much easier than you could before, so he built that just for himself to make the simulation part easier.”

But simulation alone isn’t enough, according to Goldberg. Simulation matters to the whole approach of using agents to code robots.

“The agent needs a simulator to be able to basically iterate and see how to improve this code,” he said. Goldberg noted that the existing tools “were not very reliable and had a lot of problems.”

The harness converts a VA task specification into a computation graph, optimizes it via self-learning in simulation, and hands G* to an edge-based interpreter that drives the robot — sim and real feedback close the loop. | Credit: UC Berkeley

Agents write and test code

Agentic robotics operates in a loop: Agents write robot code, test it in simulation, see where it fails, and revise. That loop is only as good as the simulator behind it.

Newton Physics, the open-source physics engine that UC Berkeley chose, is powerful but exposes hundreds of parameters, which has kept many developers from using it.

RoboSim Studio made those parameters tractable, and that turned the simulator from a bottleneck into something an AI agent could tune on its own.

UC Berkeley developed the VABAR benchmark suite with NVIDIA Isaac Lab-Arena open-source policy-evaluation framework and the Newton physics engine. It includes a detailed physics-based simulation for contact-rich robot-object interactions.

VABAR evaluates how robots perform on practical manipulation tasks ranging from tool sorting and handing to cable insertion and routing. The tool facilitates comparisons and measures progress across realistic industrial tasks, changing conditions, and increasing levels of difficulty.

Each task includes standardized variations, difficulty tiers, and success metrics, allowing researchers to measure progress, compare approaches, and evaluate whether systems can handle the demands of industrial operation. At the same time, Isaac Lab-Arena enables large-scale systematic evaluations across changing task conditions.

Spencer Huang, director of product for robotics at NVIDIA (and son of CEO Jensen Huang), has worked with Goldberg’s lab at UC Berkeley to interface with the NVIDIA product teams.

The partners listed some of the new capabilities:

  • Graph structure: Each node (perception, grasp, motion planning) can be assigned to its own agent, so agents work in parallel without “stepping on each other’s toes.”
  • ROS equivalence: The graph turns out to be equivalent to a ROS graph and can be converted to ROS 2.
  • Output: Python that calls existing vendor modules (such as KUKA) for low-level drive control. It does not replace robot controllers.
  • The harness: Thousands of prompts and structures constrain the agents.

How do agents change robot programming?

When asked how this new approach differs from straight “vibe coding” of an app, Goldberg responded that the magic is in the harness provided by GaP. The graph structure organizes the agents.

The code produced by “vibe coding” is already mature and well understood, he explained. The use of AI to write code is accepted in software engineering today. But rarely does an application function as intended in the first pass.

This is true for software from human engineers, and it’s equally true for software development developed with AI. Testing and iteration are needed to optimize the application, said Goldberg.

When applied to robotics, the best practice now is to test in simulation before deploying the code on a real robot. With agentic AI, a robotics engineer can enable the agent to iterate on both the simulation environment and then the subsequent code to more efficiently develop the robotic application.

For instance, Bosch is evaluating agentic robotics for diverse industrial automation scenarios. “Agentic robotics holds great promise because it generates interpretable code that engineers can thoroughly analyze before production deployment,” said Liu Ren, senior vice president and AI fellow at Bosch Research. “Bosch Research is actively collaborating with Goldberg and Huang and their teams.”

“AI-powered industrial robots must continuously improve reliability and performance,” said Jeff Mahler, co-founder and chief technology officer of Ambi Robotics. “Agentic robotics converted production data into robot behavior updates, increasing throughput across our U.S. fleet while keeping engineers in control.”

Goldberg is also an advisor to Ambi Robotics.

Robot data combined with predictive analytics can improve uptime and productivity, says ATS. Source: Pexels, Advanced Technology Services

Factories are adding more robots because they can handle repetitive, precise, and physically demanding work at high speed. As robotics take on a greater share of production, keeping those systems available becomes more important.

The International Federation of Robotics (IFR) reported about 5 million industrial robots in operation worldwide in 2025, up 11% from the prior year.

An unexpected robot failure can affect more than one machine. It can interrupt a cell, slow a line, and create delays that spread through the plant. As manufacturers rely more heavily on robotic systems, the need to identify developing problems before they force equipment offline becomes increasingly valuable. 

Why robotic systems raise the support stakes

Traditional preventive maintenance follows a schedule based on time, usage, or manufacturer recommendations. That approach still has value, but it may not reveal what’s happening inside a robot between planned service intervals. A joint, reducer, motor, or controller can begin to show signs of wear while the robot is still operating. 

 Predictive maintenance uses equipment data to identify changes that may point to developing faults. NIST describes condition monitoring as the detection, diagnosis or prediction of faults and failures in industrial equipment. 

For robotics, that means maintenance decisions can be based more on actual equipment condition than on a calendar alone.

Submit your innovation now!

What predictive maintenance can monitor 

Industrial automation and related systems generate many types of operating data. Useful signals depend on the robot, application, and failure mode. Common examples include vibration, temperature, and motor current. Torque, controller alarms, cycle data, and maintenance history can also provide useful context. 

The goal isn’t to collect every available data point. Teams need data that can reveal changes tied to the way a robot operates. A rise in vibration may point to a mechanical issue, while changes in motor current or torque may indicate added resistance or abnormal loading. Temperature variations can also signal that a component isn’t operating as expected. 

Changes in an end effector, sensor, conveyor, or surrounding process can affect robot performance. Looking at the robot in the context of a larger workcell can help teams separate normal operating variation from a change that may deserve maintenance attention. That distinction is especially important if the same robot handles different loads, speeds, or motion paths. 

This is where reliability monitoring can help. Sensors and connected systems can gather machine data, while monitoring and analytics tools help identify changes in equipment behavior. When a pattern changes, maintenance teams can then investigate the cause before a failure forces the robot offline.

Changes in equipment performance, plus environmental or process data, can provide warning of problems, says ATI. Source: Pexels, Advanced Technology Services

Turn robot data into maintenance decisions

Collecting data is only the first step. The information has to support a practical maintenance decision. A useful alert should help a team determine what needs attention, how urgent the issue is, and when the robot can be inspected without causing an unnecessary production interruption. 

This becomes more important as factories operate larger fleets of robots. Maintenance teams may not have time to inspect every asset at the same frequency. Predictive maintenance can help direct attention toward equipment showing signs of change while allowing healthy assets to remain in service. 

Earlier warnings can also improve parts planning. If a component shows signs of deterioration, teams may have more time to confirm the problem, locate the correct replacement part, and schedule work during a planned maintenance window.

Earlier warnings can reduce downtime and improve productivity, says ATS. Source: Pexels, Advanced Technology Services

Getting ahead on productivity, asset life, and safety

The value of predictive maintenance goes beyond preventing unplanned stops. Finding issues early on can limit secondary damage and help manufacturers get more useful life from robotic assets. Planned repairs can also reduce the disruption that occurs when technicians must troubleshoot a failed robot during production. 

A planned maintenance window gives teams more control over when equipment is taken offline and serviced. That can support safer maintenance practices because technicians can prepare for the work instead of responding to an unexpected failure under production pressure. 

As more factories rely heavily on robotics, maintenance strategies need to account for how those systems perform throughout their service life. Predictive maintenance gives manufacturers a way to use equipment data, condition signals and analytics to identify developing issues earlier. When that information leads to timely inspection and repair, manufacturers can reduce unplanned downtime, protect robotic assets and keep production schedules more stable.

Rob Carbone is vice president of operations at Advanced Technology Services. He is responsible for leading initiatives that help manufacturers improve equipment reliability, maintenance excellence, and customer success.

An autonomous mobile robot or AMR may cross dozens of Wi-Fi coverage zones during a single shift. Each transition creates a small but potentially consequential communications problem: How does the robot find its next access point without interrupting the connection it is already using?

The answer matters because AMRs, industrial inspection robots, warehouse automation, and healthcare service robots increasingly depend on continuous connectivity for sensor data, telemetry, and control.

In a conventional Wi-Fi architecture, the primary communication radio must periodically stop transmitting and receiving application traffic while it searches for alternative access points. That creates a tradeoff among connectivity, latency, power consumption, and roaming performance.

A dedicated scan architecture separates network discovery from application traffic. The robot can monitor its wireless environment continuously while the primary radio maintains the active connection.

One implementation, Synaptics Scan Core, uses a low-power wireless subsystem to monitor neighboring access points while the primary Wi-Fi radio remains dedicated to application traffic. This separation can support faster roaming decisions, lower latency, reduced packet loss, and more efficient scanning.

As robots become more mobile, roaming is mission-critical

Robots are becoming more connected and autonomous across manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, retail, and service environments. As they move through larger and more complex facilities, reliable wireless connectivity and fast roaming become core design requirements rather than secondary networking considerations.

Unlike stationary Wi-Fi devices, robots move continually between coverage areas while maintaining video, AI inference, telemetry, and fleet-management communications. These combined demands make mobile robotics a strong use case for dedicated scanning architectures.

Modern robots also support increasingly demanding wireless workloads, including HD and multi-camera video, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), AI-assisted navigation, predictive maintenance, and remote operation.

Wireless connectivity has therefore evolved from a convenience into a critical operational subsystem.

Submit your innovation now!

Mobility poses challenges

A mobile robot must maintain application traffic as it moves between Wi-Fi coverage zones. A warehouse robot may roam dozens or even hundreds of times during a shift. Each roaming event can introduce:

  • Increased latency
  • Packet loss
  • Video disruption
  • Delayed control responses
  • Reduced productivity

Common performance targets for robotics deployments include:

Requirement Typical Target
Roaming latency <80 ms
Sustained throughput 20 Mbps
Packet loss during roaming <2%

For many autonomous systems, meeting these targets is important to safe and efficient operation.

Key requirements and pain points

Although stakeholders evaluate robotics systems differently, several wireless performance measures consistently emerge as critical.

Roaming latency

A typical roaming process includes the following steps:

  1. Network discovery
  2. Candidate evaluation
  3. Authentication
  4. Security key exchange
  5. Reassociation

Each step adds delay. In robotics applications, excessive roaming latency can affect navigation, fleet coordination, teleoperation, and machine-vision performance.

Packet loss

Even brief connectivity interruptions can affect AMR operations and data transfer. Robots often require communications performance that is consistent and predictable enough for real-time operation.

Power consumption

AMRs must continuously balance battery performance and energy efficiency. Aggressive scanning improves roaming responsiveness but typically increases power consumption.

Dense RF environments

Warehouses, factories, airports, and hospitals often contain many access points, multiple wireless protocols, and significant RF reflections. These conditions place additional demands on roaming algorithms.

Dedicated scanning can address mobile robot connectivity

Traditional Wi-Fi clients use the primary communication radio for both application traffic and network discovery. During a background scan, the radio temporarily leaves its serving channel to look for neighboring access points, interrupting active traffic and potentially adding delay or packet loss.

A dedicated scan architecture assigns continuous monitoring of the wireless environment to a separate low-power resource. The primary Wi-Fi radio can remain focused on application traffic while candidate access points are identified in advance.

Source: Synaptics

Synaptics Scan Core is one implementation of this general architectural approach. A dedicated scan resource removes this contention between active communications and network discovery.

Source: Synaptics

Traditional Wi-Fi versus Scan Core

Conventional Wi-Fi Dedicated Scan Core
Main communication radio performs scanning Dedicated Scan Core performs scanning
User traffic interrupted during scans User traffic radio is not interrupted by scan operations
Reactive roaming Proactive roaming
Higher scan power Lower scan power
Longer roaming time Faster roaming
Periodic access point discovery Continuous AP discovery

Key benefits

  • Continuous network awareness: The scan radio continuously monitors neighboring channels while the primary radio remains connected.
  • Faster roaming decisions: Candidate access points are discovered before signal quality degrades.
  • Lower packet loss: Active communications continue during background scanning.
  • More predictable performance: Roaming behavior becomes more consistent and predictable.
  • Improved power efficiency: Background scanning can be optimized without disrupting active communications.

Instead of waiting for connectivity to deteriorate, the wireless subsystem can prepare for the next roaming event while application traffic continues on the primary radio.

Measured Scan Core benefits

Synaptics said its platform characterization measured substantial improvements in scanning efficiency:

Metric Improvement
Scan time Up to 65% faster
Overall scan duration Approximately 40% shorter
Scan power Up to 75% lower
Scan current Up to 77% lower

Source: Synaptics robotics platform characterization

In a mobile robot, these improvements can contribute to faster roaming, lower scan energy, longer battery life, and steadier application traffic. Actual results will depend on the platform, network topology, traffic load, and RF environment.

Applying dedicated scanning to mobile robots

Commercial connectivity platforms are beginning to incorporate dedicated scanning. For instance, Synaptics offers an integrated platform combining Wi-Fi 7, dual Bluetooth 6.0, and IEEE 802.15.4, as well as multi-band operation across 2.4, 5, and 6 GHz.

Within that platform, Scan Core provides a dedicated scan resource that operates independently of the primary WLAN subsystem. This allows scanning and active communications to occur simultaneously rather than compete for the same radio.

Multi-band awareness

The platform evaluates candidate access points across multiple frequency bands, helping the robot maintain connectivity as it moves through a facility.

Fast channel switching

The architecture supports rapid transitions between the main and scan resources. On the Synaptics robotics validation platform, switching between resources was measured on the order of microseconds.

Roaming test results

Figure 3 summarizes the minimum and maximum measured roaming times across three representative scenarios. In Synaptics platform testing, all results remained below the 80 ms target while continuous 20 Mbps UDP traffic was maintained:

Source: Synaptics

Wireless mobility becomes part of robot performance

As AMRs take on more complex workloads and operate across larger, denser environments, wireless mobility becomes part of the robot’s performance envelope. Roaming affects productivity, fleet efficiency, the user experience, and, in some applications, safe operation.

Conventional Wi-Fi makes the communication radio divide its time between application traffic and network discovery. A dedicated scan architecture separates those functions, allowing the robot to identify its next connection without interrupting the one it is already using.

Dedicated scanning and Wi-Fi 7 enhanced Multi-Link Single Radio (eMLSR) address different parts of wireless mobility. Dedicated scanning improves awareness of nearby access points; eMLSR improves how the device uses multiple links. Together, they can make roaming faster and more predictable without forcing designers to trade application performance against network awareness.

In Synaptics internal validation, eMLSR delivered up to a 10x latency improvement over single-link operation under congested conditions. Results vary with network topology, traffic load, and RF conditions. eMLSR can provide many multi-link operation latency benefits without requiring multiple fully active radios.

Synaptics says Scan Core can help mobile robots maintain coverage. Source: Synaptics

Glossary

Autonomous mobile robot An AMR can navigating and performing tasks using sensors, AI, and wireless connectivity without requiring fixed guidance infrastructure or direct human control.
Access point An AP is a wireless networking device that provides Wi-Fi connectivity to client devices within a coverage area.
Enhanced Multi-Link Single Radio eMLSR is a Wi-Fi 7 capability that enables a single radio to intelligently utilize multiple wireless links, improving latency, reliability, and power efficiency.
Fleet management Software and network infrastructure used to monitor, coordinate, and manage multiple AMRs operating within the same environment.
Latency The time required for data to travel between devices. Low and predictable latency is critical for real-time robotics applications.
Multi-Link Operation MLO is a Wi-Fi 7 feature that allows communication over multiple wireless links, improving throughput, reliability, and network efficiency.
Packet loss Data packets that fail to reach their destination. Excessive packet loss can interrupt video, telemetry, and real-time control.
Roaming The process by which a Wi-Fi client transitions from one access point to another while maintaining network connectivity.
Scan Core A dedicated low-power wireless receive subsystem that continuously monitors the wireless environment while the primary Wi-Fi radio remains dedicated to application traffic. By separating network awareness from communications, Scan Core enables faster roaming, lower latency, reduced packet loss, and improved power efficiency, according to Synaptics.
Simultaneous Localization and Mapping SLAM is a navigation technique that enables a robot to build a map of its environment while simultaneously determining its own position within that map.
Simultaneous Transmit and Receive STR is a Wi-Fi 7 Multi-Link Operation mode that enables simultaneous transmission and reception over multiple wireless links, maximizing throughput and reducing latency.
User Datagram Protocol UDP is a lightweight transport protocol used for real-time applications such as video streaming, voice, gaming, and telemetry. Unlike TCP, UDP does not retransmit lost packets, making it well suited for measuring network latency, packet loss, and roaming performance in wireless systems.
Wi-Fi 7  The latest generation of Wi-Fi technology (IEEE 802.11be) introduced features such as MLO, wider channel bandwidths, lower latency, and improved efficiency in dense wireless environments.

About the author

Mikko Niemi is a product manager for wireless products at Synaptics Inc. He has more than 15 years of experience across industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), semiconductor, and software-as-a-service (SaaS) sectors. Niemi specializes in building and scaling intelligent, data-driven platforms that power connected infrastructure, smart energy systems, and next-generation industrial applications.

He previously worked at Lantronix, where he led a portfolio that included industrial IoT gateways, cloud-based, SaaS device management platforms, and global connectivity services—delivering edge-to-cloud systems that integrate real-time telemetry, AI/machine learning analytics, and robust security at scale. Niemi previosly held management roles at Silicon Labs and Landis+Gyr. He holds an MBA and a Master’s in electronics engineering.

The Advanced Robotics for Manufacturing, or ARM Institute last week said that that its member consortium has grown to include more than 500 organizations nationwide, with thousands of individual subject matter experts represented within these organizations. The organization collaborates with its consortium and the U.S. government to promote the U.S. as leading nation in manufacturing output through the adoption of robotics and AI.

“We are proud to work with our consortium to build a resilient, secure, and bright future for U.S. manufacturing,” stated Jorgen Pedersen, CEO of the ARM Institute. “Our member consortium is the foundation of our Institute and integral to our mission.”

“Our members have collaborated with us on hundreds of technology projects, helped us launch major initiatives, including our national workforce resource RoboticsCareer.org, supported manufacturers through their robotics and automation journey, and more,” he added. “We look forward to celebrating this milestone at our 10th Annual Member Meeting later this month.”

“The ARM Institute’s member consortium is expansive, bridging gaps and bringing varied perspectives together to catalyze robotics, physical AI, and workforce solutions to strengthen U.S. manufacturing,” stated the organization.

Last month, the institute issued a project call from the U.S. Navy to address needs in the shipbuilding industrial base. This month, the ARM Institute put out a request for proposals for a skills gap analysis for a localized talent supply chain to support the organic and defense industrial base.

Its consortium members include manufacturers of all sizes, defense contractors, technology providers offering robotics and AI systems, research universities, community colleges, vocational schools, government entities, startups, and others.

ARM Institute membership is at the organizational level and provides access to funding opportunities, member-exclusive events, a digital member community for virtual collaboration, and more. ]]> Danish startup Memora has raised €1.7 million (DKK 13 million) to connect cemetery managers, gardeners and families through one platform, bringing together administration, maintenance and communication.

The round was led by venture capital firm True Collective. Chris Evans, formerly of Kahoot!, will also join the company as CTO in early 2027.

“I learned how much of the work that takes place in a cemetery is never seen by the families, and gained an understanding of both the gardeners’ daily routines and the needs of the families. Today, we develop the platform together with cemetery managers, gardeners and families, and their experiences are crucial to us,” says Johan Toft-Nielsen, founder and CEO of Memora.

While finding a direct or adjacent comparator is difficult, Memora’s funding can be placed alongside a series of European investments in digital end-of-life services and operational management software in 2026.

In Sweden, Solace Care raised €2.1 million to expand its digital platform for end-of-life planning and bereavement support, while Ireland-founded EstateMin secured €1 million for its AI-powered estate administration software. In Denmark, Copenhagen-based Cortas raised €1.47 million to develop its AI-native property management platform, while Cyprus-founded Piney secured €1.6 million for its rental property operations business.

EU-Startups has previously examined European DeathTech companies offering digital memorials and bereavement administration, providing an earlier reference point for Memora’s combination of cemetery operations and family communication.

“The opportunity isn’t just to replace paper with software,” adds Chris Evans, CTO at Kahoot!. “It’s to rethink how an entire industry operates, from the cemetery office to the people on the ground and the communities they serve. AI opens up possibilities that simply didn’t exist a few years ago. We’re building around those possibilities, not the limitations of yesterday’s systems.”

When Johan Toft-Nielsen founded Memora in 2022, the company sold grave maintenance directly to thousands of families. Its own gardeners cycled between cemeteries with backpacks and shovels while relatives followed the work in an app.

But doing the work themselves revealed a bigger opportunity: building better technology for the people running cemeteries.

Today, it is the cemeteries that purchase the platform, and their own gardeners who carry out the work. The solution has been developed in close collaboration with cemetery managers, gardeners and families.

Cemetery managers can plan and assign tasks, gardeners document work through their phones, and families receive photographs and community updates when graves are cared for. Families can also share memories of their loved ones through the platform.

Memora is already using AI to turn gardeners’ work into updates for families, reducing administrative effort while improving communication. The company is bringing modern technology, geospatial tooling and AI into an industry still dominated by manual processes.

“We invest in founders who earned their insight the hard way. Memora has turned former competitors into partners by listening to cemeteries and developing the solution together with them. The team has demonstrated its ability to turn those insights into a digital platform that cemeteries every day in their daily operations. Memora understands both daily life at the cemetery and the technology, and with Chris Evans on the team, Denmark is only the beginning,” says Rolf Pedersen, managing partner at True Collective.

With the new capital, Memora aims to bring its approach to cemeteries across Europe, where millions of grave plots are still managed through manual and fragmented systems.

Deal count hit […]

The post OPINION: Long sales cycles could be FinTech’s biggest competitive advantage appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Any FinTech founder raising in the UK this year will have seen the numbers – according to KPMG’s Pulse of FinTech, investment fell to €2.1 billion (£1.8 billion) in the first half of 2026, down around two-thirds on the same period last year and the lowest since the report began in 2016. Deal count hit a ten-year low. The capital that is still moving is going to AI, and within AI it is going to where the results can be seen fastest. 

Alongside the numbers runs a story: AI has collapsed the sales cycle. Products that used to take a year to sell now close much more quickly, and founders who can’t match the pace should question whether they are building the right thing, or building it in the right country.

For anyone selling into regulated financial services, the story is a little different. Worse, believing the first version of the story is one of the fastest ways to put a good company out of business. Rather than being an issue, the long sales cycle is one of the few things in this market that is a strength and cannot be copied in other industries. 

What a sale actually looks like

Here is what selling AI to a mortgage network, a wealth manager or an advice firm actually involves. It means integrations into systems that were not built with an innovative AI provider in mind. It means lengthy security reviews, several boards and committees, each on its own calendar. It takes several internal sponsors, who need to be won over separately and who do not all agree with each other. You also need trust in the system, trust in the output, and the certifications to prove it, from the usual ISOs through to the new AI equivalent, ISO/IEC 42001.

In the UK at least, the procurement cycle has not sped up. Regulated financial services firms are accountable to the FCA for what their systems decide, a point the regulator’s own Mills Review made quite plainly this summer, and in compliance much of the work is straight-through: a file review or a financial promotions check is either right or it is a regulatory problem. A highly regulated product, with many integrations, that has to pass several boards and several sponsors, moves as slowly as it always has. The sales cycle is long, and that is fine and normal.

Founders arriving with consumer expectations miss this. They hear about the fastest sales cycle in AI without noticing that the companies telling that story are B2C, or B2B businesses that behave like B2C. The lesson travels but the conditions do not.

Surprise is what kills a startup, not the cycle

A long cycle only becomes dangerous when it is a surprise. If a founder expects deals to close in weeks and sizes their future round, their hiring plan and their investor conversations around that timeline, the business can find itself in real trouble by month nine, with nothing closed and no fault in the product. If the cycle is a known quantity from day one, it is simply a parameter to design around.

Designing around it means a few unglamorous things. Size rounds so the money lasts through more than one full cycle. Hire people who have sold into regulated institutions before and know that a fourth meeting with the risk committee is normal rather than a warning sign. Set investor expectations before the term sheet, not after the first missed quarter – and get the certifications done early, because the security review will ask for them either way.

Our investors describe the length of our sales cycle as a moat, and they are right. The entrants it protects against are the naive ones, and in this market they are usually people from inside the industry – they have very good product knowledge, a real understanding of the problem yet no experience of how running a startup works. They build something credible, start selling, and run out of money before the first contract lands. The technology can be copied and the domain knowledge is widely held. Being set up to wait is the hardest thing to copy, because it has to be built into the funding, the hiring and the expectations from the beginning.

Build in the slow lane, and build it here

The other conclusion founders are drawing from the funding numbers is that conditions will be better in the US and while for some companies it is, for others it would be wise to question what they are actually aiming to build before making that move. The most compliance in the world is in Europe, not America: the most demanding regulators, the most complex rulebooks, and the customers with the strongest reason to buy. Leaving the market where your problem is most prominent, because the deals there take longer, is a strange trade. The US may not be the answer for everyone.

The slow lane has three things going for it. There are fewer competitors, because most cannot afford to wait and many of those that do try, fail. The customers you win stay, because a firm that has just spent a year taking you through three committees has no appetite to repeat the exercise with someone else. And the market rewards the one thing that is hard to fake: a company designed, from its first round, to survive the wait.

FinTech is not dying. Parts of it are, but companies using AI to do work that firms could not do before are growing quickly but selling slowly. The nine-month deal is not a flaw in regulated FinTech. It is the entry fee, and the founders still standing in two years will have paid this on purpose. 

The post OPINION: Long sales cycles could be FinTech’s biggest competitive advantage appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Swiss SpaceTech startup SWISSto12 and French startup UNIVITY are advancing Europe’s ambitions for sovereign satellite communications after successfully completing a Critical Design Review (CDR) for two active antenna systems designed to deliver 5G connectivity from space.

The milestone brings the companies closer to demonstrating broadband and direct-to-device connectivity through a single satellite architecture, combining European satellite manufacturing expertise with a homegrown approach to space-based telecommunications infrastructure.

The collaboration brings together two startups that have attracted significant investment in 2026.

Switzerland-based SWISSto12 secured €73 million in January from European Space Agency member states for its HummingSat programme, and then closed a €61 million Series C in July. While Paris-based UNIVITY raised €27 million in April from Blast, Expansion, the Deeptech 2030 fund managed by Bpifrance on behalf of the French State, and two family offices.

Emile de Rijk, CEO and founder of SWISSto12, says: “UNIVITY set us an ambitious schedule; reaching Critical Design Review in less than one year was possible due to SWISSto12’s proprietary and differentiated payload and antenna technology and a vertically integrated delivery model. It’s a significant milestone for the program and the start of the next phase as we move into hardware production and an extensive verification and acceptance campaign.”

Founded in 2011 by Emile de Rijk as a spin-off from his doctoral research at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne (EPFL), SWISSto12 specialises in satellite payloads, antenna systems and compact geostationary satellites, using proprietary manufacturing technologies including 3D printing. UNIVITY, founded in 2022 by Charles Delfieux and previously known as Constellation Technologies & Operations, is developing a Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO) satellite constellation designed to enable telecom operators to extend their existing 5G services into space.

At the centre of their collaboration are two active phased-array antennas being developed by SWISSto12 for UNIVITY’s 5G non-terrestrial network (NTN) demonstration satellites. The first, an S-band direct radiating array, is designed to connect standard 5G smartphones directly to satellites. The second, a Ka-band antenna operating at 26 GHz, will support broadband services and feeder links connecting satellites with terrestrial infrastructure.

By integrating both capabilities into a single satellite, UNIVITY aims to enable telecom operators to provide broadband and direct-to-device services under their own brands, complementing existing terrestrial networks rather than replacing them.

The development forms part of UNIVITY’s uniShape programme, supported by France 2030 and the French Space Agency (CNES). The programme aims to demonstrate high-throughput, low-latency 5G connectivity using VLEO satellites, with the longer-term objective of developing a shared, neutral space infrastructure that enables European and international telecom operators to maintain greater control over their connectivity services.

For SWISSto12, the partnership puts its HummingLink antenna and payload technologies to work on a European connectivity project. The company manufactures passive radiating antenna components through 3D printing, integrating miniaturised, low-loss filters with beamforming electronics and digital controls. Design and manufacturing are carried out at its Swiss facilities, providing a vertically integrated process from technical specifications through to finished hardware.

Completing the Critical Design Review means the antenna designs can now progress towards hardware production, verification and acceptance testing. While the milestone does not yet demonstrate operational connectivity in orbit, it represents a step towards validating a satellite architecture capable of supporting two different 5G services simultaneously.

Charles Delfieux, Chief Executive Officer of UNIVITY, adds: “Active antennas are central to our 5G payload architecture: they will enable a single satellite to deliver both broadband and direct-to-device connectivity. This dual capability is essential to our ambition of providing telecom operators with a shared space-based infrastructure that complements their terrestrial networks. By reaching this milestone in less than a year, SWISSto12 has demonstrated its ability to support our ambitious roadmap for the uniShape program.”

Their collaboration comes amid broader investment activity across Europe’s SpaceTech sector. In October 2026, EU-Startups highlighted financing announcements exceeding €1.3 billion across a selected group of European companies, including €450 million in primary financing for Finland’s ICEYE and €387 million for Germany’s The Exploration Company.

Investment has also reached smaller startups developing technologies essential to future space operations. Switzerland’s Stellar Alpina raised €3.8 million to develop propulsion systems for in-space mobility, while France’s ArcSpace secured more than €2 million to advance technologies for satellite servicing and repair.

Against this backdrop, the SWISSto12–UNIVITY collaboration illustrates how European startups can combine specialised technologies to develop more independent space infrastructure. Rather than relying on a single company to manufacture satellites, develop payloads and operate connectivity services, their partnership brings together complementary capabilities across borders.

Their progress could help establish whether Europe can turn its growing investment in SpaceTech into infrastructure that provides greater technological and commercial autonomy.

The funding was led by Mérieux Equity Partners, with NRW.BANK and Boehringer Ingelheim Venture Fund joining the syndicate as co-leads. ]]> SRTD Biotech, a Jülich-based BioTech startup focused on developing next-generation precision mRNA therapeutics, has completed an oversubscribed €31.5 million Seed financing round.

The funding was led by Mérieux Equity Partners, with NRW.BANK and Boehringer Ingelheim Venture Fund joining the syndicate as co-leads. Lilly Ventures, HTGF, and the Freiburg-based family Office Anobis Asset also participated in the Seed round.

“We believe SRTD Biotech has the potential to redefine what is possible with mRNA therapeutics. Its highly differentiated technology addresses one of the key challenges facing the field today: achieving precise, selective therapeutic activity while limiting effects on healthy cells. 

“Having worked closely with the company to strengthen its strategy, build its leadership team and establish a scalable platform, we are delighted to lead this financing with our Mérieux Innovation 2 fund (MI2) alongside an exceptional group of investors,” said Kristin Thompson, Director at Mérieux Equity Partners. 

Founded in 2019 in Jülich by Dr. Bernd Hoffmann and Dr Heribert Bohlen, SRTD has developed an approach to cell-specific messenger RNA (mRNA) expression using intracellular RNA disease markers that activate the mRNA expression exclusively within target cells.

The company notes that these selectively expressed RNA (seRNA) constructs enable the controlled expression of therapeutic payloads within diseased cells, while minimising exposure in healthy tissue.

With this novel approach, SRTD plans to create safer, more effective, and differentiated RNA therapies that overcome limitations of non-selective mRNA expression and the constraints of targeting cell-surface proteins. 

SRTD is an integrated RNA therapeutics company combining three technology platforms: proprietary seRNA technology; a novel fusogenic LNP delivery platform to access the liver, lung, brain, and other organs; and a synthetic biology platform with bioinformatics and AI-driven RNA design capabilities. This integrated technology platform provides an end-to-end solution for generating differentiated RNA therapies across a wide range of therapeutic areas and indications.

After the financing round, Matthias Alder was appointed SRTD’s Chief Executive Officer. He has held senior C-suite roles (including CEO, COO and CBO) at publicly traded BioTech companies in the US and Europe. 

“The proceeds will enable SRTD to advance Bernd’s vision of delivering safe, effective, and differentiated RNA therapeutics to patients whose diseases remain inadequately addressed by current therapies,” said Alder.

Along with Matthias Alder, Dr. Heinz Koeppl has joined SRTD’s leadership team as the company’s Chief Technology Officer and the founder of SRTD’s synthetic biology platform. He is also a professor at the Technische Universität Darmstadt and the director of its Centre for Synthetic Biology. 

Together with Dr. Hoffmann, Dr. Koeppl will lead the scientific strategy of SRTD, with a particular focus on RNA marker identification and AI-based construct optimisation to ensure the selective and efficient activation of seRNA constructs.

Most recently, Dr. Jens Hennecke joined the executive leadership team of SRTD as its Chief Business Officer. He is responsible for driving business development and strategy, seeking to leverage the company’s platform through R&D collaborations in therapeutic areas and indications beyond SRTD’s own product pipeline.

“SRTD Biotech shows how cutting-edge research from North Rhine-Westphalia can open up new ways to treat many diseases with significant unmet medical needs. Bringing innovations like these from research into medical practice takes capital. With our investment in SRTD Biotech, we are helping a highly innovative company develop a promising new technology in NRW and scale it internationally from here,” Johanna Antonie Tjaden-Schulte, Member of NRW.BANK’s Managing Board. 

NRW.BANK is participating in SRTD Biotech’s financing round through its NRW.Venture EU Tech&Scale fund. Under its InvestEU partnership, a guarantee agreement with the European Commission enables the Düsseldorf-based bank to invest a total of up to €200 million in additional funding in young scale-ups through the fund.

Free open-source software, which can be used, modified, and redistributed under its license, can help founders ease the squeeze. It lets a small startup build products that once required a large engineering department. But a shortcut is not a strategy. To make good […]

The post OPINION: Building open source gives startups a head start, not a moat appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Every startup faces the same squeeze: big ambitions, small team and limited budget. Free open-source software, which can be used, modified, and redistributed under its license, can help founders ease the squeeze. It lets a small startup build products that once required a large engineering department.

But a shortcut is not a strategy. To make good use of open source, founders must decide what they should build themselves, what to borrow, and which skills their team needs to retain. Here is what to consider, from saving time and standing out to staying secure and talking to investors.

Saving time

Microsoft’s Edge browser shows how this can work. I co-authored a study of its move to Chromium, the open-source engine also behind Google’s Chrome, found faster releases and closer alignment with Chrome’s supported web features. Edge remained Microsoft’s own product, on a shared foundation. For founders, the question is how much development work a shared foundation can save, and what trade-offs come with it.

Artificial intelligence offers a similar shortcut. Free toolkits such as TensorFlow and PyTorch help developers build AI applications. “Open-weight” models, such as Meta’s Llama, DeepSeek and Qwen, let teams download an AI system that has already been trained and adapt it, rather than start from scratch.

But open-weight does not necessarily mean open source. Founders should read the license carefully: downloading a model does not necessarily provide access to its training data or unrestricted rights to sell products built on it.

Before committing, startups should build a small prototype around a real customer task. A polished demo can hide missing features, thin documentation or fiddly integration work. Founders should also factor in the costs of computing power and upkeep. Access to the code lets teams tailor software or run it in a customer’s own systems, provided they have the skills and resources to manage it.

Standing out

If competitors can use the same technology, a startup needs to give customers a reason to choose its product. That might mean specialist features, smoother links with the systems customers already use, or reliable support. Founders can use the development time saved to find out what customers value enough to pay for.

Take an AI tool for manufacturers. It could pair a widely available model with a factory’s equipment records and tests designed around how engineers work. Tying the technology to a real job can make a product useful even when the model underneath is available to everyone.

Some companies make money from their own open code. Strapi, a French startup, offers a free content management system and charges for extra features and support. Founders who publish their code need to be equally clear about what customers pay for. They also need to allow time for users’ questions, documentation and outside contributions.

Keeping expertise in-house

Startups need staff who understand how the product works and can change it. In research I led on German firms, I found that product innovation was strongest among companies that outsourced a moderate amount of IT work. In related research I co-authored, we found that excessive reliance on outsourcing raises the risk of intellectual-property infringement.

The practical question for founders is which skills they need to retain as they draw on outside work. Early choices can become expensive to reverse. A team learns one framework; data takes on its format, and other parts of the product grow around it.

Before the business relies on a critical component, the team should test how easily it could be replaced. Design decisions and the ability to investigate failures should stay within the team. When working with outside developers, founders should agree who owns the work and what stays confidential.

Engineers also need time to experiment. If all their effort goes into stitching together other people’s software, they may struggle to build the know-how needed for the startup’s next product.

Maintenance and security

Joining an open-source community can help a startup’s developers learn. Research on larger companies found that contributors got more value from using open source, partly through feedback from other developers.

An active community can help spot and fix problems, but security still needs an owner inside the startup. 

The Open-Source Security Foundation advises tracking outside components, checking their origins and maintenance, and monitoring newly discovered vulnerabilities. Someone within the startup should be responsible for testing and installing updates.

Some popular projects rely on a single volunteer. Paid support may be worthwhile for critical components, while startups publishing their own code also need time for handling security reports and maintaining new versions.

Making the case to investors

Founders should show what the head start delivered, whether they have a working product, paying customers, or evidence of demand. They should explain what they didn’t have to build because they used open source, and what they developed themselves.

Our study found that US startups that engaged with outside projects on GitHub, a popular code-sharing site, were more likely to have raised their first funding round. The link was stronger for novel technologies and weaker in crowded markets. However, the research does not imply that publishing open source code alone will win over investors.

Founders should be ready to explain their own contribution to the product, the cost of maintaining it and how they would manage problems with a critical dependency. The test is whether open source helps them build something customers value while leaving the team able to maintain and improve it.

]]> Calogena, a French nuclear startup developing a small modular reactor (SMR) designed to supply low-carbon heat to district heating networks, has secured €40 million.

The funding came in the form of a grant from the European Commission’s Innovation Fund ,and it marks the first time that European funding has been given to an SMR earmarked for the direct construction of a commercial facility.

“This funding marks a major milestone for Calogena. Having developed our technology and brought it to industrial scale, we are now entering the construction phase of our first commercial reactor,” said Julien Dereux, Executive Chairman of Calogena.

Calogena was founded in 2021 as a subsidiary of Groupe Gorgé, a Paris-based high-tech industrial group with approximately 3,500 employees and €600 million in revenue. The company is developing a 30-thermal-megawatt, water-cooled SMR specifically designed to decarbonise district heating networks.

Its reactor is based on pool-type research reactor technology, a design proven in hundreds of installations worldwide. It operates at low temperature (100°C) and low pressure (6 bar), less than a bicycle tyre, making it simpler and safer to operate than conventional power reactors.

Another strength of Calogena’s SMR is its compact footprint, requiring just 3,000 square metres of land and under 1,000 square metres of building. The design also does not require major water or electricity supply, and refuelling requires only one lorry delivery every two years. Each module can supply heat to around 20,000 households and produces less than 80ml of nuclear water over a lifetime of use.

The grant follows more than €50 million already secured under France’s national industrial strategy programme, France 2030, which helped the company develop its technology and bring it to industrial readiness. 

The €40 million grant will be used to fund the construction of Calogena’s first commercial reactor in Pierrelatte, which would serve as the company’s inaugural commercial reference project. The company says the town will receive locally produced, low-carbon heat, an alternative to the carbon-intensive and largely imported energy sources that currently account for nearly one-third of Europe’s total energy demand. 

“The European Commission’s support confirms the maturity of our project and its potential to address one of Europe’s major energy challenges: producing local, low-carbon, cost-competitive heat at scale while strengthening energy sovereignty. Pierrelatte would be our first commercial reference and should pave the way for wider deployment across Europe,” added Dereux.

In addition to the Pierrelatte project, the company is also pursuing projects across Europe and is in contention to supply more than fifteen reactors in Finland, where it opened a subsidiary in 2025. In June, Calogena signed a cooperation agreement with Veolia, a European leader in district heating, to explore the deployment of its SMRs across Central and Eastern Europe.

As the European district heating market is projected to reach around 1,000 TWh by 2050, Calogena argues that its technology can provide a price-stable, long-term solution for energy sovereignty. It is targeting initial deployments from 2030, with its first commercial reactor in Pierrelatte scheduled to go live in 2032.

]]> Marble Imaging, a Bremen-based big data Earth Observation (EO) company setting up Germany’s first commercial constellation of very-high-resolution (VHR) satellites, has raised an additional €6 million in a Seed extension round led by Cherry Ventures. 

In December 2025, the company announced it had closed an oversubscribed €5.3 million Seed round led by High-Tech Gründerfonds, bringing total funding to €11.3 million.

“To make better decisions, data access must be immediate and actionable. Europe and many of its global partners lack this capability today. We at Marble are determined to close this gap, and Cherry’s trust helps us achieve this faster,” said Robert Hook, co-founder and CEO of Marble Imaging. 

Founded in August 2023 by Hook, Dr. Gopika Suresh, Alexander Epp, and Dr. Raul Scarlat, Marble Imaging is building its constellation of VHR satellites to provide up to hourly EO data and analytics for time-critical insights of the planet.

According to the company, the data and derived EO-based analytics will be vital in supporting rapid decision-making for defence, climate security, crisis and disaster management, green and sustainable energy transitions, infrastructure and mobility, and more.

It already offers advanced data analysis services, including object detection for situational intelligence, terrain analysis and trafficability assessment, coastal asset monitoring and land cover classification.

Marble highlighted that although VHR imagery is a core input for security and commercial intelligence, Europe and many of its partners rely on non-European providers. “This makes them vulnerable to being cut off from coverage over key areas of interest, as materialised in Ukraine or the Strait of Hormuz, creating massive economic as well as security knowledge gaps,” it stated. 

Marble is therefore setting up Germany’s first commercial constellation of very-high-resolution (VHR) satellites. The German startup is also building an AI-powered analytics platform that converts multi-source data into insights. It also notes that as Marble’s constellation scales, the interplay of these segments will create a uniquely well-trained AI solution that delivers actionable decision support for users in the defence, civil security, and critical infrastructure sectors, and beyond.

“Europe needs its own eyes in space, and Marble Imaging is building them. They are using AI to turn pixels into answers, exactly what government and defence customers need. This team has spent their careers in the industry and knows what it takes to build something very big. The product Marble will deliver doesn’t exist in Europe yet, but we’re convinced it has to,” said Filip Dames, Founding Partner at Cherry Ventures.

Marble’s first satellite, Marble Sat-1, is fully funded, has completed pre-flight testing and is scheduled to launch in early 2027. It is designed to capture imagery at up to 0.7 m spatial resolution in the visible and near-infrared spectrum and will also gather data in the shortwave infrared spectrum. 

The company plans to use this capital to accelerate the scaling of its constellation, with a goal of 30 satellites by 2030. It will accelerate satellite and launch procurement for Germany’s first commercial very high-resolution constellation

“Scaling from here is a question of capital, not technology. The demand is proven, the hardware comes from experienced suppliers, and our software is already used by paying customers. We need to invest in more satellite capability in space, and this round accelerates our path to delivering sovereign intelligence with a European identity – stable access, transparency and democratic governance that partners around the world can count on,” said Hook.

]]> Authorities publish final reports for only about half of aviation accidents investigated under international rules, an International Air Transport Association (IATA) executive has said. The reporting gaps make it harder for airlines and regulators to identify hazards that could lead to similar accidents elsewhere.

Mark Searle, IATA’s global director of safety, told Reuters that he saw little improvement in publication rates. “I don’t think 50% is acceptable,” he said, speaking on the sidelines of the International Aviation Safety Summit in Montreal. “It just seems ​we’re floating around that 50% and there’s no real sort of forward trajectory.”

Hassan Shahidi, president and chief executive of the Flight Safety Foundation, which organised the summit, told Reuters that investigating bodies often cite a shortage of staff with the expertise to complete reports. He said some cases are also politically sensitive, including suspected aircraft downings.

What IATA’s accident data shows

IATA’s 2025 Annual Safety Report found that investigations had been completed for 63% of the 203 accidents it recorded from 2019 to 2023. 

The association has set up a database of safety recommendations from accident investigations. 

This gives operators a way to discover findings that apply to their own fleets or procedures. For example, a report can give an airline enough detail to review whether its training addresses the circumstances that led to an accident involving another operator.

What investigators must publish after a year

The International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) sets out the investigation process in Annex 13 to the Chicago Convention. The state conducting the investigation must make the final report public as soon as possible and, if possible, within 12 months of the occurrence.

If the final report is unavailable after 12 months, the investigating state must publish an interim statement on each anniversary. The statement should describe the progress of the investigation and any safety issues it has raised. A preliminary report shares early factual information, generally within 30 days, while investigators still gather and analyse evidence.

Before publication, the investigating state circulates the draft final report to the states entitled to participate and gives them an opportunity to comment. Investigators can issue urgent safety recommendations while that work is underway.

The final report brings together the evidence, analysis, conclusions and any safety recommendations so others can see how the findings were reached.

Air India Flight 171 final report still pending

India’s investigation into Air India Flight 171 shows how the interim reporting process works. The Boeing 787-8, bound for London Gatwick, crashed shortly after take-off from Ahmedabad on 12 June 2025. The crash killed 260 people on the aircraft and on the ground.

India’s Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau published a preliminary report in July 2025 and issued an interim statement on the first anniversary. In that update, the bureau said it was continuing to analyse evidence. As AGN reported at the time, families were still waiting for the investigators’ conclusions a year after the crash.

Reuters reported on 12 November that the timing of the final report remained unclear. When published, the findings will give families and the aviation industry the investigators’ account of what happened and set out any recommendations arising from the evidence which could prevent a similar tragedy in the future.
